that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for financial assistance to the Atlantic provinces by authorizing the payment, out of the consolidated revenue fund, for each of the four fiscal years commencing on the first day of April, 1958, of an annual grant of seven and one-half million dollars to each of the provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Newfoundland, and an annual grant of two and one-half million dollars to the province of Prince Edward Island, and also to provide as an interim measure that in its application to the fiscal year commencing on the first day of April, 1958, the definition of "standard individual income tax" in the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act, shall for the purposes of that act and any agreements made thereunder be read and construed as if for the words "10 per cent" therein there were substituted the words "13 per cent".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to the present resolution and to the bill which it is hoped will follow upon the passage of the resolution, the government attaches very great importance, for it looks upon this measure as one that will bring aid to the provinces and municipalities of this country, and effective aid also in meeting the problem of unemployment. The terms of the resolution, I think, are clear. It is the hope of the government that it may be possible after adoption of this resolution to proceed with the motion for second reading of the bill tomorrow.
Fiscal relations between the dominion and provincial governments in this country are very largely governed by the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act of
1956.	Apart from the subsidies provided for by the British North America Act, it is this statute which almost entirely governs the fiscal relations between the dominion and provincial levels of government in this country. Therefore, Mr. Chairman, in approaching this problem it was necessary for the government to take account of the fact that here is an existing situation. By the terms of the legislation arrangements were created for a five-year period, and pursuant to the statute agreements had been entered into between the former government and the governments of nine of the provinces.
Sir, I do not need to remind the house that those who compose and support the present government had in 1956 in the debate on that measure opposed it because they said it was inadequate in the provisions it had made for
Dominion-Provincial Relations the provincial share of the revenues from what are called the joint fields of taxation.
The act deals with the distribution, as between the dominion and provincial levels of government, of three sources of revenue; personal income tax, corporation tax and the succession duty. The act makes provision for three types of sharing. It first takes those three types of taxes called the standard taxes and provides that the provinces may by agreement receive from the federal collection of income tax 10 per cent of the personal or individual income tax collected, nine percentage points of the corporation tax and half the succession duty. That applies to the three standard taxes.
In the second place, the act provides for equalization payments. It takes the average of the two top provinces of the per capita yield from the standard taxes and makes provision for a federal grant, an equalization payment, designed to bring the per capita yield in each province up to that average.
Then there is a third form of grant or payment, namely stabilization. The purpose of the stabilization payment was to assure to all the provinces that none of them would lose in 1957, in the quinquennial period then beginning, any of the benefits they enjoyed under the agreement and legislation existing from 1952 to 1957. It happens that up to the present only two provinces, namely Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, have derived benefit from the provision of stabilization, but that provision is there as a guarantee to all the provinces.
Now, sir, none of the provinces was satisfied with the division of those revenues; none of them. We pointed that out in the discussions of this matter on July 23 and later, 1956. If there was any doubt of that in the mind of any hon. member he had only to attend the dominion-provincial sessions last November to realize that the provinces were quite dissatisfied with the provisions thus made.
I should like now to say a word concerning the November dominion-provincial conference, sir. The new government did not lay before that conference any hard and fast formula. It sought in the first place to create a new atmosphere, feeling that a new atmosphere was necessary and desirable if there were to be hope of achieving settlement of the outstanding fiscal problems between the two levels of government. The provinces were therefore invited to propose whatever it suited them to propose, and they did all respond.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
The Prime Minister did lay before the conference three particular suggestions indicating that in respect of those matters the federal government was prepared to take a course of action in compliance with the wishes of the provinces. In the first place he indicated the willingness of the present government to abolish the so-called threshold limit on unemployment assistance; in other words the provision that federal contribution to unemployment assistance should begin only when unemployment exceeded .45 per cent of the population in any province. In the second place he proposed that what amounted to a veto of a majority of the provinces on the application of hospital insurance in any province should be abolished. In the third place he indicated that the federal government was prepared to subscribe to and introduce an Atlantic adjustment grant.
There was discussion of these matters at the conference, and there was discussion of course of other matters. The provinces put forward freely their views on the wider question of the division of revenues from the three standard taxes. There was discussion of the extent of hospital insurance, and there was considerable discussion on federal-provincial co-operation in the development of national resources. At the conclusion of the two days which had been set aside for it the conference, as had been indicated well in advance, adjourned. The fruits of the conference I think fully justified the laudatory comments made upon the conference in all parts of Canada by a number of provincial premiers and by the press. I point out that an atmosphere was created from which one could be hopeful that when the conference is resumed there will be a good chance of arriving at a fiscal settlement.
Then, too, a communique was subscribed to by all the heads of government attending which has some significance with respect to the matter I should now like to discuss, namely the Atlantic adjustment grants. I feel it is a tribute to their breadth of vision and to their sound Canadian approach to the problem of the Atlantic adjustment grants that the provinces in other parts of the country put no obstacle in the way of proceeding to give recognition to the fiscal needs of the Atlantic area. They subscribed to this term in the joint communique:
It was generally agreed that the over-all economic position of the Atlantic provinces is now such as to justify some special grants in aid to the governments of those provinces from the federal government.
In other words there was general agreement that the fiscal position of the Atlantic provinces is such that there should be some

special consideration given to those needs in any reallocation of the revenues from the joint fields of taxation, or the standard taxes. Consideration had been given at the 1956 conference to a formula put forward by Premier Hugh John Flemming of New Brunswick on this subject. The essence of that formula in a word was that where the per capita income in any province falls below 85 per cent of the national average, that province should qualify for some special assistance. It happens that all four of the Atlantic provinces fall below that 85 per cent. This was very clear evidence that the formula was sound, and indicated the necessity of some special action for the benefit of the Atlantic provinces. This formula was based upon a five-year average for the years 1952 to 1956 inclusive, taking the population in the ages 15 to 69 inclusive as a basis for calculating the working population and determining the average personal income. Various elaborations of that formula had been prepared. The formula had commanded not a little discussion at the 1956 conference.
Following the adjournment of the dominion-provincial conference of November last, federal officials met together with representatives of the four Atlantic provinces and, I am happy to say, arrived at a formula that was unanimously accepted by the four Atlantic provinces after due consideration. Here again I think tribute is due to those who represented these provinces and sought to arrive at agreement.
This agreement was that any amount provided out of the federal treasury by way of Atlantic adjustment grant should be divided amongst the four provinces on this formula: Nova Scotia, 30 per cent; New Brunswick, 30 per cent; Newfoundland, 30 per cent and Prince Edward Island, 10 per cent. This left to be determined only the amount which the federal government was prepared to allocate to Atlantic adjustment grants out of the total yield from these standard taxes.
We decided, Mr. Chairman, that the amount we would recommend to parliament would be $25 million per annum. This figure was not simply taken out of the air. As a matter of fact it was very close to the figure that had been discussed on previous occasions when this original formula was put forward by Premier Hugh John Flemming. There were various ways in which the result of that formula had been worked out, and the one which had been most discussed arrived at a figure of $24,833,000, so we decided that $25 million, as the nearest round amount, was a sound figure to place before this parliament with the government's recommendation.

In the result, therefore, if parliament gives approval to the resolution and the bill to follow, the Atlantic provinces will receive in the four remaining complete fiscal years of the five year period covered by the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act and the existing agreements, $100 million. The $25 million in each of these fiscal years will be divided in the following amounts: Nova Scotia, $7.5 million; New Brunswick, $7.5 million; Newfoundland, $7.5 million, and Prince Edward Island, $2.5 million.
One does not need to argue the fact that the Atlantic area deserved special fiscal consideration. The fact that this point was conceded by the other provinces leaves, I am sure, no room for argument on the subject. The government therefore, Mr. Chairman, believes that in submitting this proposal to parliament we are submitting a proposal that is fully justified by the economic facts of life in Canada; that will commend itself to the sense of fair play of Canadians in all provinces, and will assist in the Atlantic area of Canada in the development of resources, in enabling these provinces to raise the level of public services up to a point where they are comparable with those prevailing in other provinces of Canada, and will assist as well in the provision of employment.
I think I need say no more upon this subject of the Atlantic adjustment grants. I stress that we have given consideration to all aspects of the matter, and the bill that will follow will make clear the binding provision for the four fiscal years commencing April 1 next, and will extend throughout the entire lifetime of the federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements act and the nine agreements that have been entered into with nine provinces pursuant to the provisions of that statute.
I now turn to the broader subject of fiscal relations between the federal government and the ten provincial governments. This government has made it very clear, Mr. Chairman, that it has no thought of imposing any dictate upon the provincial governments. At no time will this government adopt any take it or leave it attitude. As I indicated earlier, we approached a situation where agreements had been entered into by nine of the provinces, and where those agreements had another four years to run and the legislation under which they derive their authority had the same period to run.
This session of parliament has extended far beyond expectations and, as I do not need to remind hon. members, the sittings of this parliament have been very onerous and protracted. We have now been sitting, since about the beginning of December,
Dominion-Provincial Relations morning, afternoon and night and on Saturdays as well. In the face of these facts and the burdens that have had to be discharged in relation to the business that has been brought before the house; and the fact-let it not be forgotten-that we are only a minority government, it was impossible to reconvene the conference while parliament was in session and pursuing such a rigorous schedule of sittings. While we have been waiting hopefully to see some approach to the end of the session, it became quite clear latterly that there was no hope of concluding the session in time to reconvene the conference in time to arrive at conclusions or agreements in time to permit the provincial treasurers of the provinces to prepare their budgets for the forthcoming year.
As to the legislatures of the provinces, at least one of them has been in session for some time, and I think virtually all of them are being called to meet within the next several weeks. We did not need to be told how urgent was the need on the part of the provincial governments of knowing what they might expect to receive and take into their budgets in the forthcoming fiscal year commencing April 1.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, as it became impossible to reconvene the conference in time to allow that to be done, the government decided that what needed to be done in the emergent situation was to provide as an interim measure some additional basis upon which the provincial treasurers could proceed to budget for this forthcoming fiscal year. Therefore in the second branch of the resolution we propose a measure which will be of benefit to all ten provinces of this country. It will assure for the fiscal year commencing April 1 next an additional sum of $62,203,000 for distribution among them on the relatively simple basis of increasing from 10 per cent to 13 per cent that proportion of the individual income tax which the provinces are entitled to receive.
There are many detailed calculations on all aspects bearing upon this matter which have been reduced to a table by the officials of the Department of Finance. If I had the leave of the house to do so I should be glad to propose that this table might be placed upon Hansard.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
I wish to make several observations about the nature of the provisions made in the resolution. The grants are unconditional. The provinces, however, have always represented that they needed an enlarged share of the revenues from these standard taxes in order to help their municipalities. Indeed, some of the provinces have gone further and have said they would use any additional provision made for them from this source to help municipalities.
There are therefore three conclusions that I think we are entitled to draw from this additional provision. The first concerns the municipalities, of which in this country there are approximately 4,500. We recognize the burden carried by these 4,500 municipal governments and the fact that they operate on a limited and, in a jurisdictional sense, static tax base. The financial health of the municipal governments has a good deal to do with home ownership. We are concerned about housing. We are concerned about the shortage of serviced land. We must be much concerned about the increasing burdens that are carried by the municipal governments in making provisions for educational facilities, roads and services, whether pertaining to land or social services. Therefore we consider we have every reason to look upon this present measure as a powerful aid to the municipal governments of this country.
A second observation relates to the provinces. We recognize the heavy burdens carried by the provincial governments of this country and the extent of their constitutional burdens. We who now sit on this side of the house have said before that too much of the tax dollar is going to the federal government. We respect the constitution; we are federationists, not centralists, and we must take into account the fact that the burdens carried by the provinces in the matters of education, highways, social services, etc., have been increasing in almost astronomical proportions. The burden of developing the resources in this country, so closely related to our prosperity in Canada, also rests in a jurisdictional sense, with the provinces, and we know that the growth of population in this country and the rapid development that have taken place in recent years have greatly added to the burdens borne by the provinces. This is best evidenced in those provinces where growth has been most rapid. We therefore consider we have every reason to believe that this measure will greatly aid the provinces.
The third matter I wish to mention is unemployment. The provinces and the municipalities are very important sources of employment and work in this country. There is very much work, undoubtedly, that needs to

Dominion-Provincial Relations be done in the provinces and the municipalities, and work done at the local level has this advantage: it does not uproot the unemployed and carry them elsewhere. It seeks to provide work where unemployment does already exist. The municipalities, particularly, have been hampered and restrained by high costs and difficulties of borrowing in recent years, and on them has fallen much of the burden of the tight money policy which has been prevailing in the past several years. That tight money policy has now been eased in line with the policies of this government, but we go further and say we believe that these funds now made available in this way will provide something better than easier loans or easier credit; they will provide grants. Therefore we look, through this measure, for the early amelioration of unemployment as the result of a works program to be commenced by the provincial and municipal governments.
In conclusion, there are several matters which I feel I should mention by way of clarification of the points which may occur to hon. members, perhaps foreshadowed by some of the questions asked last Saturday morning when this measure was announced in the house. In the first place, there is no increase in taxes involved in the present measure, no increase in taxes whatsoever. It is a tax-sharing, and not a tax-raising measure.
In the second place in at least one province it will have the effect of reducing taxes; and here I may say to my friend the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount, in expanding the answer I gave him on Saturday that the third statutory change, in addition to the two indicated in the resolution, will be in the form of an amendment to the Income Tax Act which will be introduced by the government at the next session of parliament, namely a measure to amend section 33 of the Income Tax Act by changing the figure 10 per cent therein to 13 per cent in order that the taxpayers of the province of Quebec may derive the full benefit of the deduction of 13 per cent. In that case it will apply to the tax rates in effect in 1958.
The third matter I would mention concerns the equalization principle. We have carried forward in this measure full recognition of the principle of equalization now embedded in the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act. Indeed, of the $62 million provided a little over $17 million is ascribable to the equalization principle; and the equalization principle, as in the statute, is still tied to the average of the two provinces in which the per capita income is highest in

Canada. Therefore let there be full recognition of the fact that the equalization principle has retained its full recognition in the proposals now put forward.
The fourth matter concerns Newfoundland. This measure has no bearing whatever upon the present inquiry of the royal commission on the terms of union with Newfoundland.
Fifth, the provinces will still have the benefits of the tax yields calculated prior to the reductions which were brought about by this house in response to the government's tax reduction program last December. In other words the percentages payable to the provinces-this increase from 10 to 13 per cent- will be calculated on the basis of the rates in effect last year.
As my concluding observation, the present measure, bringing as we consider it does belated justice to the Atlantic area and belated assistance to all the provinces, carries the principle of the recognition of the fiscal need of the provinces further than it has ever before been carried in Canada's history.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I hope the rosy expectations of the Minister of Finance with respect to the effects of the increases proposed in this legislation will be justified because whether we sit on this or the other side of the house, we are all equally concerned with the economy of our country. I may say at once that it is the intention of the official opposition to support both the increase in the direct tax revenue sharing with all the provinces and the special grants to the Atlantic provinces.
I wish to make a few observations on the proposed increase of general application under the direct tax revenue sharing arrangements, but I will leave the subject of the Atlantic provinces grants to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate and other members of the opposition.
Of course no one can deny that during the war and ever since the war it has been an unavoidable necessity for the government of Canada to derive a substantial portion of its revenues from taxes on personal incomes, corporate incomes and, to a lesser degree, in succession duties. It is, I think, also obvious, and has always been obvious to everyone, that the burden of provincial and municipal treasuries has been rising because of the rapid growth of our population which requires increased provincial and local services and because of the increased costs of maintaining and expanding those local services.
It will be remembered that at the close of the war under the wartime arrangements, when all the then nine provinces were included, the provincial revenues from the

direct tax fields were about $100 million. For the present fiscal year the provincial revenues from the same fields, including equalization payments, were estimated by Mr. Harris at approximately $630 million when the subject was before the house for consideration in 1956.
From the table which the Minister of Finance has now placed on record in Hansard I gather that the total standard taxes, equalization and stabilization payments for the present fiscal year without the increase would be $630,878,000. That is an increase of considerably more than six times what it was at the end of the war. The proposal made in 1956 was that there should be an increase of approximately $114 million in the payments for the present fiscal year, over and above what it would have been, calculated on the basis of the 1952 formula. That is considerably more than the total increases which are proposed in this resolution, a resolution we are prepared to support.
The purpose of the present government in its tax revenue sharing arrangements is the same as the purpose of the previous government. It has always been recognized that it was proper that there should be some portion of the revenues available from these direct tax sources available for provincial services, and more than once I had occasion to state what was the government's policy in this regard. One of those occasions took the form of a letter addressed to all of the provincial premiers on January 14, 1955, in which I expressed it in the following words:
The present government has no intention of abandoning the objective of the tax-rental agreement which is to make it financially possible for all provinces, whatever their tax base, to perform their constitutional functions themselves and to provide a reasonable Canadian level of provincial services without an abnormal burden of taxation. That is the foundation of the policy of the federal government.
In the arrangements we proposed in 1956 a genuine endeavour was made to go as far as the situation at that period allowed toward achieving that objective.
At the present time the government feels it is possible to go beyond what was done then. The amount of the increase proposed is less than what was approved by parliament in 1956 but it is, of course, in addition to what was then being provided. It is being done by modifying one of the percentage rates in the formula which is the basis of the 1956 legislation.
We considered that formula was a good formula; that it provided for bringing up for each province the theoretical yield from taxes in this field of direct taxation to the average that proved to be the yield for the
Dominion-Provincial Relations two provinces in which it was the largest. We note with satisfaction that the equalization principle is to be maintained, and is regarded as the proper basis for the arrangements to be made in regard to this tax revenue sharing proposal.
During this session we have not, of course, had a national budget, and we are not therefore in a position to see accurately just how this will fit into the whole budgetary situation of the country at this time. That is the responsibility of the government, and I assume that the government has been fully conscious of that responsibility and of the effect on the budget of this and all the other substantial increases in permanent charges which have been made.

speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman permit me to remind him that there is nothing in these proposals which affects the current fiscal year? They will come into effect only in the fiscal year commencing April 1 next. And there will, of course, be a budget introduced for that year.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I appreciate that these provisions are designed to take effect in the case of the special grants for four years, beginning with the year 1958-59, and the other case for the fiscal year 1958-59 as an interim provision pending whatever other decisions may subsequently be made.
We do know, however, that the burdens of the provinces and local authorities have been increasing, and we do know that there have been changed conditions. When this formula was prepared it was regarded as a formula which should be adhered to, at least until something better could be found to deal with the situation; but it was understood that the percentage rates might very well be changed as conditions and needs changed. We do know that the needs of the local authorities are substantial, and we hope they can make good use of these additional funds in order to provide needed services and needed employment.
As I have said, we intend to support the measure, notwithstanding the procedure followed by the government in dealing with the provinces. With respect to that, I think it is well to remind ourselves of the contrast between the manner in which this has been dealt with at this time and the manner in which it was studied throughout 1955 and 1956 to bring about the tax revenue sharing arrangements which were incorporated in the statute of 1956. I shall merely point out what were the various steps taken in order to bring about an arrangement which, though it was not satisfactory in the amount it provided to the provinces, was on a basis which was declared by all the representatives of the provinces at the time to

Dominion-Provincial Relations be better and fairer than anything which had been devised up to that time in this regard.
The first move that was made in respect to the discussion of these federal-provincial fiscal arrangements was a letter I addressed to the premiers of all the provinces on January 14, 1955. It was on the lines that arrangements were being proposed for unemployment assistance to those who were not covered by the Unemployment Insurance Act, but at the same time it called attention to the fact that it was necessary that there should be a dominion-provincial conference before the end of 1955 in accordance with the terms of the agreements which had been in effect since 1952, and it contained the following paragraph:
It had always been understood that it would be necessary to hold a federal-provincial conference before the end of 1955 to discuss fiscal arrangements for the years which will follow the present tax rental agreements. In the light of recent developments it might be the desire of the provincial governments to have this conference held at an earlier date.
I shall accordingly communicate with you again shortly after my return from the commonwealth prime minister's meeting in London towards the middle of February with a view to working out arrangements for a conference at a time which will be satisfactory to all governments concerned.
I am referring to letters that were tabled at the time. I wrote suggesting that we might have this preliminary meeting for this purpose on April 21 and 22 if those dates were satisfactory to everybody. Further communications made it apparent that April 26 and 27 would be more convenient dates for this conference, and it did take place on those dates. It was then determined that there would be other conferences in the meantime to deal with the unemployment assistance problem, and that the formal conference to deal with federal-provincial fiscal matters would meet here on October 3. In the meantime there were meetings of officials to prepare the data for the conference. One of them, attended by provincial officials, met in July, 1955, in Ottawa and another was held in Halifax in September, 1955. The conference met and sat in open session on October 3, and then sat in committee for the three following days.
The matter of fiscal relations was carefully gone into at that conference. It is quite true that there were representations made by the premier of New Brunswick with respect to the advisability of there being a special grant for the Atlantic provinces. Similar representations were also made by Mr. Hicks, the then premier of Nova Scotia, and the matter was given careful consideration at that time.
On January 6 I wrote to all the premiers outlining the recommendations that the government would take the responsibility of making to parliament in that regard. This was


followed by further correspondence, as a result of which there were some modifications made in the proposals that were recommended to parliament. There was another meeting with the provincial premiers here in Ottawa on March 9, following which a revised outline of the proposals was addressed to each of the premiers on March 19, 1956. The legislation was introduced in July of 1956, and debated and adopted at that time.
The procedure adopted by the present government was much more summary than that. There was a two-day conference here, which I would imagine from the rosy expectations that had been raised by the declarations made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign it was felt would settle the fiscal relations between the federal government and the provinces.

I recall that there was correspondence tabled at that time, but during the election campaign it was suggested by the Prime Minister that this matter would be settled to the satisfaction of the provincial governments if the hon. gentleman's party achieved office. There were some of these promises which those of us who knew how these things could be done would have discounted, but which do not appear to have been discounted to the same extent by the general public, and they apparently were not intended to be discounted to the same extent by the general public.
The conference was held, and the Minister of Finance says there was no take it or leave it proposal put before it. In fact there was no proposal at all suggested. It is a very convenient excuse to say there were going to be no take it or leave it suggestions. The conference adjourned to meet again early in the new year. Well, it has not met early in the new year, and the prospects at the present time do not seem to indicate that it is going to meet at any time that could be considered early in the new year, if it meets at all within the first half of the new year.
The government is now attempting some implementation of the objectives that had been suggested during the campaign. It has

decided that it would recommend these immediate increases. When we come back we shall use whatever good things there are in the policies of the present government, because they are not provided for a party; they are provided for the good of the country at large, and when they are such as to operate for the good of the country at large it is quite proper and laudable that they be made use of by those who have the responsibility of furthering the welfare of the country. But this is an added reason for our being prepared not only to go along with and support those increases but to accommodate the government, as the other parties have done, in making it possible to deal with this resolution expeditiously, without requiring that the usual notice called for by the rules be observed.
I think there will be general satisfaction in the fact that the present circumstances have been recognized as such as to require that this addition be made. With respect to the special grants to the Atlantic provinces, they are matters that did receive serious consideration but which had not up to that time been expressly agreed to by the representatives of the other provinces. A letter from the premier of Manitoba dated December 18, 1957, which has been printed as an appendix to Hansard, seems to indicate that it must be a great surprise to him that this matter
Dominion-Provincial Relations is being finally dealt with before the general policy of the fiscal arrangements applicable to all the provinces has been determined or let alone approached.
As I recollect the terms of that letter, it was felt that although the situation in the Atlantic provinces migh be somewhat unique at this time, whatever was done there should be in accord with a formula that could, if and when circumstances made it applicable elsewhere, also be extended to such other provinces. But these are details. What is important at the present time is to make this amount available, which I hope will produce some of the benefits of relieving the unemployment situation at the present time to which the Minister of Finance alluded.
However, though the economy of the country has been operating in terms very much larger than any of the amounts that can be fitted into a dominion-provincial fiscal arrangement, I hope that these amounts will produce something toward the very much desired objective of getting the economy back to the condition under which it was operating less than a year ago.

Mr. Chairman, when we too indicated our readiness to proceed with this resolution today without requiring the further 24 hours delay that the rules stipulate, that implied our readiness to support the legislation that the government proposes to bring before parliament at this time. We are prepared to give it our support because it is clear that the provincial governments are in need of additional revenues. Since this is the time of the year when provincial treasurers are preparing their budgets, it is desirable that they know at the earliest possible date what sums of money they can count on by way of payments under the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act. Hence we shall vote for this measure.
May I also say at the outset that we are particularly pleased to support a resolution that proposes special grants for the Atlantic provinces. All of us in Canada appreciate the contribution made by those provinces and their people across the years to the development of this country, and in view of their special needs at this time we think it is appropriate that special adjustment grants should be provided for the four provinces down by the sea. Nevertheless, Mr. Chairman, there are some comments that we feel need to be made at this time.
First of all I want to say a word with respect to the basis upon which these special grants are being made to the Atlantic provinces. I speak as a spokesman for a party that is keen on something being done for

Dominion-Provincial Relations those provinces, but we think it should be done on the basis of a formula, on the basis of a principle, rather than a lump-sum handout decided upon by the government of the day. This smacks too much of the practice of charity and gets too close to the practice of political hand-outs at a particular time in the affairs of the nation.

speechtext: Shame.

heard the word "shame" from across the way. I suggest that if there is any shame it is to be heaped upon the government for once again putting the Atlantic provinces in the position that they are getting a form of charity rather than something which is their right on the basis of a principle adopted by parliament.
I go all the way with the premier of my province and the premier of Saskatchewan, who along with others in the country have been saying that something should be done for the four Atlantic provinces and that it should be done on the basis of a formula, taking into account the per capita income of the various provinces, so that when the per capita income is low in the Atlantic provinces they will get special adjustment grants as of right, and so that if the same situation obtains in any other provinces those provinces will also get the special adjustment grants.
It seems to me that the present government has adopted a very unwise course so far as this matter is concerned, bearing in mind not only the rights of the situation but also the sensitivities of the people of the Atlantic provinces. Since my own forbears came from the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, I think I can make that reference.
The other comment I wish to make is this. I am surprised that our friends across the way chose to deal with this matter on a completely unilateral basis. This is particularly surprising in view of some of the comments the Minister of Finance as well as the present Prime Minister, the Minister of National Revenue, and the former leader of the Conservative party, Mr. Drew, made in 1956; and I shall remind them of some of their words in a few moments.
The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister both say this government is not handing this arrangement to the provinces on a take it or leave it basis.
The hon. member for Quebec East put it very well when he pointed out that the present government did not present anything to the provinces on November 25 on a take it or leave it basis; they did not present anything at all. However, they are now presenting to the provinces the proposition which

is in the resolution before us and this proposition is being presented on a unilateral basis; it is being presented to the provinces on a take it or leave it basis.

This is the same gentleman, now Minister of Finance, who as the hon. member for Eglinton on July 23, 1956, as recorded at page 6296 of Hansard, said this:
There is no use, so far as Her Majesty's loyal opposition is concerned, asking us to approve a form of dominion-provincial fiscal arrangement which has not received the approval of a single provincial government.

Nonsense, my eye. The present minister carried out that opposition by voting against second reading of the bill and by voting for a six months hoist on third reading which was moved by the hon. member for Peace River.
I point this out to the Minister of Finance as well. I attempted to ask him a question in the middle of his speech, and I thank him for his courtesy in sending me a note to explain the matter. My question related to the discrepancy between the figures the minister gave on Saturday as the amounts of money the provinces would receive, and the figures contained in the table which he [DOT]placed on Hansard today. The figures as to the total amount to be received by the provinces are different in all 10 cases. In eight instances, let it be said, the provinces will receive a little more according to today's figures than they would have received according to Saturday's figures. In so far as two provinces are concerned, Prince Edward Island and British Columbia, they will receive less according to today's figures than they would have received according to Saturday's figures.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
The Minister of Finance has given me an explanation which is valid and which I accept, namely that the figures on Saturday did not take account of the stabilization payments. In other words, over the weekend the figures have had to be corrected in accordance with the threefold aspect of the formula upon which these amounts are calculated. It is all very fine for the minister to be able to explain this to us today. I point out to him that, so far as the provincial governments are concerned, all they have had to go on over the weekend is the figures they saw in the newspapers on Saturday. The government of British Columbia assumed from what they saw in the newspapers on Saturday that they were receiving an increase amounting to something of the order of $5,563,000 as a result of this change. They will learn from the newspapers today that instead they are going to receive an increase of only $2,842,000. In so far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, they learned from the newspapers on Saturday-perhaps they got the telegram, I do not know-that they would receive a total increase of $2,870,000. They will learn from the press today that the total increase will be only $2,500,000.
I suggest that because these increases are needed by the provinces, and needed in particular by the Atlantic provinces, we will vote for them. This unilateral action, however, is something that is rather difficult to understand from the government across the way. Listen to what Mr. Drew had to say about acting in this way when he spoke in the house on July 16, 1956, as recorded in Hansard at page 5995:
What has happened in this case is unhappily typical of what has happened on other occasions. It illustrates the unfitness of this government to govern.
The words of Mr. Drew come wafting across the Atlantic ocean to his party which is now in power.
The Minister of Finance has told us that there were meetings from time to time starting on April 26 of last year and then finally coming to a meeting on March 9 of this year. That should never have been dignified with the name of "conference". All that amounted to was that this government called the provincial premiers together for one day so that they might be told what this government was prepared to do.
At least the Liberals had the courage to call the provincial premiers here and tell them to their faces what they were being given. This government tells them by means of a telegram without knowing whether all the 10 premiers received that telegram. Mr. Drew went on:
That is not a conference in any meaning of the word "conference". It is certainly not the type of conference that accepts in fact or in principle the

Dominion-Provincial Relations relation of the federal and provincial governments or the place of the provincial governments under that system. It was said by more than one provincial premier that this was no conference at all. It was said that they could just as well have stayed away and been told by a letter what this government was prepared to do.
Once again it was a case of "take it or leave it".
Mr. Drew's successors did not do it by letter, as he suggested it could have been done by the Liberals; they did it by telegram which the premiers may or may not have received. Listen also to what the present Prime Minister said on July 24, 1956, as recorded at page 6370 of Hansard:
I believe this. I think it is fair to say that the attitude taken by the government at the last conference was an arbitrary one. The government simply said, "These are the terms." No opportunity was given for amendment or for amelioration of any terms. The recipe for a division of taxation was as final as the laws of the Medes and the Persians; and how similar that attitude was to the attitude of the government in this house, which is that power makes perfect anything they do.
Oh, how quickly our friends across the way have learned to act in that same manner.
There was no opportunity for negotiation; there was simply the attitude of a feudal lord bringing into being a modern feudalism and laying down the law to the vassals.
That is not the attitude, that is not the consideration to which the provinces are entitled under a constitution which allocates powers as between the federal and provincial governments. That is not an attitude which will remove the road blocks which today deny Canada the development which should indeed be heard. I feel that even yet if there were an attitude on the part of the federal government to negotiate, terms could be achieved which would be acceptable and which would go a long way towards solving this difficult and complex problem.
I have a few more of these quotations, particularly some from the Minister of Finance, but I have already indicated his attitude so perhaps I will save the others for later on in this debate.
May I say, Mr. Chairman, that any complaints that were made against the Liberal government really can be made ten times over against this government. The Liberal government at least called the premiers down here two or three times over a period of months and if there was not complete agreement, at least the knowledge as to what was to be done was conveyed to the provinces at a meeting here in Ottawa. In this instance, as I say, it is being done on a unilateral basis by this government simply saying, "Here it is; here is what we are doing for you; take it or leave it".
I think about the weakest excuse I ever heard any responsible government make is this excuse that the federal-provincial conference could not be called together again because of the protracted sittings during this session of parliament.

It was agreed that a subsequent meeting be held as soon as possible in the new year in accordance with the proposal made by the dominion government in calling this conference.
The Conservative government was good enough to allow parliament to adjourn for a day and a night for an event which took place in this city not long ago and which, I suggest, was of much less importance than would be a federal-provincial conference. I suggest if it was possible to adjourn the house for that length of time we would have agreed readily to adjourn for two or three days or a week, if necessary, so that the important business of a federal-provincial conference could be carried on. I am still not convinced that it was necessary. Most of the federal-provincial conferences-especially the ones that have been valuable and effective-have been held while parliament was in session. I am satisfied that this job could have been done and that many people in Canada are laughing at the government for using this excuse that they could not call the conference into session again because parliament was still here.
I also want to say that I think the government is stretching a point when its ministers assert that they are proposing what is before us today because of the general agreement that was arrived at at that conference. I refer to the conference in November, 1957. I have read several times the agreed communique that was issued at the end of that conference. There was not very much that was agreed to, really. It was agreed that

certain things had been discussed, namely three: the threshold provision in the Unemployment Assistance Act, financing of hospital insurance and special assistance to the Atlantic provinces.
But in the matter of what was discussed with regard to hospital insurance, there seems to be quite a difference of opinion and the agreed communique does not resolve that conflict. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance say that what was understood was that something would be done about the date on which the act would come into effect. I welcome the fact that it is to come into effect on July 1 this year. I still think that a change in the act should be made at this session of parliament so that the provincial treasurers, in drawing up their budgets, will know they can count on that money as of July 1.
But if hon. members will read again the letter that Premier Campbell wrote to the Prime Minister under date of December 18, to which the hon. member for Quebec East referred, they will see that Premier Campbell understood that among the three things that were supposedly agreed to, so far as hospital insurance was concerned the point agreed on was the inclusion of mental and tubercular patients within the framework of that legislation. I say this to the government: You cannot have it both ways. You cannot claim you are doing what is before us today because it was agreed to at the conference and then refuse to do something else which, on the testimony of Premier Campbell and Premier Douglas, I may say, was one of the things that was agreed to at that conference. Apparently bringing tubercular and mental cases within the hospital insurance act has been forgotten, shelved or perhaps put off altogether because of the change of attitude on the part of the premier of one of the provinces of this country. But nevertheless the government used this so-called agreement as a pretext for going ahead on a unilateral basis.
I ask that the government and hon. members do what was suggested by the hon. member for Quebec East, namely that they read Premier Campbell's letter in which he points out that any agreement that was arrived at was because of the insistence of the Prime Minister that these matters be dealt with before any revision of the tax-sharing arrangements as a whole. In his letter of December 18, 1957, Premier Campbell makes it clear that this action was without any warning and that, as far as he is concerned- and Premier Douglas has taken the same position-the situation is this. Both these premiers say that so far as they are concerned, 96698-214
Dominion-Provincial Relations before you make special adjustment grants or before you do these other things that are going to take money out of the pot and affect the amount that is left for distribution you should reach agreement on the principle with regard to federal-provincial tax-sharing arrangements. I think the position taken by Premier Campbell in his letter, and supported by Premier Douglas, is a sound one. In the face of that letter, for this government to go ahead and do what is being done today on a unilateral basis is, in my opinion, a case of the government doing all the things that Mr. Drew, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance said were wrong when they castigated the former government for supposedly doing things on a take it or leave it basis.
In so far as this whole arrangement is concerned, Mr. Chairman, may I point out that Premier Campbell's letter of December 18 is not just to be sloughed off as just another of those letters, because on at least two occasions-on January 13 and January 20, to be exact-I asked the Prime Minister whether he had yet made a reply to Premier Campbell's letter. It is a lengthy letter. It goes into all these matters. It calls for anything that is to be done for the Atlantic provinces to be in the context of an over-all agreement. It is an excellent case. The first time I asked the Prime Minister the question as to whether he had answered this letter he said he would have to look up the files and find out what had been done. The second time he said that he thought his letter of acknowledgment implied that there would be a reply in substance later on. But without giving that reply in substance, or in other words without further consideration of the points made by Premier Campbell, we have this take it or leave it unilateral action today of which the provinces have learned by reading of it in the newspapers and by telegrams if by this time they have received them.
In the agreed communique of November which the Prime Minister tabled in the house on November 27, 1957 we find this paragraph:
Possible changes in the tax sharing arrangements act were discussed but it was understood that no endeavour would be made to reach conclusions on this matter prior to further consideration of the subject by the dominion government in the light of the public statements made by the provincial representatives in open sessions and the discussions which took place in committee.
Yet despite that statement, changes are now being made in the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act. I know the minister will tell me that it is only on an interim basis. It is not interim so far as four of the Atlantic provinces are concerned. Those payments are fixed for the next four fiscal years. What is fixed is not only the amount but the principle of these payments being

Dominion-Provincial Relations made on the basis of charity, on the basis of a handout by the government of the day, rather than on the basis of a principle that would say to the Atlantic provinces, "You are getting this money as a matter of justice", and would say to the other provinces that if their per capita income fell to a certain point, they would get it as well.
But, Mr. Chairman, not only has the government taken this unilateral attitude so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned but so far as all the provinces are concerned I suggest that this so-called interim basis is a fiction. Oh yes, this is interim in the sense that it applies only to one year-the fiscal year 1958-59. That means that so far as the other three years are concerned they are yet to be negotiated, but I suggest that so far as the 1958-59 agreement is concerned, this matter will drag on. A conference will not be held early in 1958, it will not be held in the spring of 1958; there will be an election in March or April and a conference will be put off until after that time, perhaps after another session of parliament, and by the time the conference is called we will be so far along in the 195859 fiscal year that it will be useless to continue to talk about the arrangements for this year. The only talk will relate to the three remaining years of the five-year agreement.
That means that at the present time the provincial treasurers in planning their budgets cannot build them up on the notion that these are interim arrangements for 195859; they will have to assume that the amount of money they are going to get out of this interim arrangement is all they will get for the 1958-59 fiscal year. They will also, of course, have to examine closely into the estimates tabled on Saturday and the estimates tabled today to determine what that amount will be.
In that connection I would point out that the provincial treasurers were told in 1956 that the new act then being put through parliament would provide them with certain moneys in addition to what they were receiving under the old agreements. I know that some of the provinces did not receive the extra amount that it was estimated they would receive; when the year actually came along experience was such that they received less. So the provinces, as I say, are in an uncertain position as to what they are going to receive but, of one thing they can be sure, no matter how much the Minister of Finance underlines the word "interim" this is on a take it or leave it basis for the 1958-59 fiscal year.
