-a Conservative government, if elected, would immediately call a federal-provincial conference to settle existing problems. The federal system was threatened by "the centralization complex of the St. Laurent government" and a healthy balance of revenues between federal and provincial governments must be assured.
These will be my last words, Mr. Chairman, since my time is up, but those people across the way had a lot to say about the percentage of the tax dollar which the federal government has been taking in years gone by. The Minister of Finance has not bothered to tell us how much that percentage is corrected by the slight change which has been made today.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is not changed at all.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The
change is so slight it does not change it at all. In other words, the conference was called, it was adjourned, and it has not been called back. All the government is trying to do is get into the position where it can check off an election promise and say, "We have kept it", when they have not done so at all. All they have done is to take this unilateral action which belies the position taken by the members of the government when they were on the opposition side of this house, and that is not good enough.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, much, at least, of the elation felt by members over the increased assistance to provinces which was announced by the Minister of Finance on Saturday, and spoken of again today, has been dulled by the way in which the offer has been made and the arrangements worked out.
My hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre has made an excellent case
96698-244i
Dominion-Provincial Relations against the way in which it has been done and I do not intend to labour what he said by any means but merely say I agree with it. There is indeed much to be said for the fact that under the arrangements for extra grants to the Atlantic provinces some figure was pulled out of the air and was offered to them as a lump sum rather than being laid down as part of a formula. I am sure all hon. members will realize there is a great difference between payments made under a formula which come to be considered as payments as of right and a hand-out which cannot be justified as part of a formula.
I suggest to the Minister of Finance that it would have been far better if he had worked out a formula and then made his payments accordingly-as has already been said-instead of the unilateral basis upon which this has been done, which is going to throw a good many of the provinces into a state of confusion.
The third thing about which I am concerned is that the new series of grants will be considered by the government as something final and that we may not get a dominion-provincial conference now for a long time. Furthermore, that this will be used as an excuse for not calling the conference back for a long time, particularly if the federal government now takes the view that it will have to budget for a deficit when it does bring in a budget, if ever. The excuse will then be given that we are spending much more than we are taking in by way of revenues and therefore we cannot countenance any requests from the provinces for a fairer share of the revenues of this country. That is the position we will get into and so it looks to me as though walls are being built to bolster the excuse that may be made if there are pleas for a fairer share of the revenue dollar of this country.
One of the things we have talked about so long in this house has been that very matter, the necessity for a fairer share of the revenue dollar so that the provinces and the municipalities can discharge the responsibilities placed upon them. They have demonstrated fully that they cannot do it in present circumstances. Along comes the government and says to the provinces, unilaterally: we will give you a 3 per cent increase and whether you like it or not you will have to accept that.
The Minister of Finance has said that he will call a dominion-provincial conference as soon as he can.
On Saturday an exchange took place between the minister and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to which I should like to refer briefly because it has a bearing on this question. As recorded in Hansard at

Dominion-Provincial Relations page 3796, the minister had just concluded a brief interchange with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The passage reads as follows:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Broader questions can best be considered when the dominion-provincial conference reconvenes.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: When will that be?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend could answer some questions I should like to ask him and his associates, it would be a great deal easier to answer questions like that. Obviously a great deal depends upon the willingness of this house to address itself to the essential business of the house and to expedite what needs to be done. We had hoped, as I indicated, that the dominion-provincial conference could have been reconvened this month, but the progress in the house has been so slow and there has been so much discussion of two or three measures that it has been impossible to take up the reconvening of the conference.
And then, as recorded on the following page, the Minister of Finance, speaking of the change in the hours of sittings had this to say:
I think the answer I gave to the last question should be enough to satisfy even the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. In November the hours of sitting were not nearly so rigorous as they have been since.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Who
changed them?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
They were brought into effect by decision of the whole house, with no objection so far as I am aware from any party in the house.
I am sorry to have to draw to the attention of the Minister of Finance the fact that when the proposal was made by the government to increase the hours of sitting I pointed out very strongly the unwisdom of this course of action. I said it would probably increase rather than decrease the length of the session, and I moved an amendment to the government's proposal. My group in the house voted solidly for the amendment and against the government's motion to lengthen the hours of sitting. Unfortunately, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre and his group voted against my amendment.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Was
the amendment not to the effect that the hon. gentleman was against these lengthened hours being continued into January? We did not think the government would go through with such a proposition.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: We were just being a little more realistic. The important thing is that the Minister of Finance was wrong on Saturday, because we did object to the lengthening of the hours and if the government had been realistic about the hours of sitting I am satisfied that not only should we have made better progress but we should have settled this matter, not on an unilateral basis but on a partnership basis of the kind we have been advocating every year for many years.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The
Tories used to advocate it, too.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes, is it not an unfortunate situation? When I was sitting on that side of the house and they were over here on my right-not on my immediate right, but jumping one-they used to talk in the same way about the necessity of introducing the partnership principle under which things would be done by conference and agreement. I do not know what has happened to them. I cannot understand it. Is there a disease over here? There must be. They have certainly caught it. I think we will have that area fumigated before we take office, because the thing is catching.
Unfortunately this will all be written into books. I suppose there will be red books and blue books from now until doomsday. That is the unfortunate part of having books; every time we speak our words are indelibly written down for all time. But I am going to say this: we will never settle this matter of the fair division of the tax revenues of this country until the partnership principle is introduced, and it is high time that some government got this into its system.
My mind goes back to another conference, one of the very first that was ever held on this question of fiscal arrangements between the federal and provincial governments. This took place in 1940 when there was held in this very chamber what was known as the Rowell-Sirois conference. It happened in the middle of winter at a time of great difficulty in the provinces. There had been a good deal of pressure brought by the provinces in favour of such a conference and the federal government, in order to placate the provinces, I think, more than anything else, had set up the Rowell-Sirois commission to investigate the financial situation in the various provinces.
Afterwards, when the report had been made, we came down from all parts of Canada to listen to the wise men in the temple of high finance. And I recall very well how the minister of finance of that day and his deputy were called out during the conference by the governor of the Bank of Canada, and a further conference took place in the hallway. Those men came back into this chamber and began to tell us what they would do, and I recall with considerable satisfaction how two men, the premier of my own province, who has been maligned for it ever since, and the premier of Ontario-Mr. Aberhart and Mr. Hepburn-rose one after the other and scotched that conference.
As I look back on that incident, on the proposals they made, and on the practice which has developed since, I thank God for

it, and if anyone wishes to get a clear idea of the developments which have taken place in dominion-provincial fiscal relations since that time to the advantage of the people of Canada, let them just look up the records and see what has happened since 1940 when the Rowell-Sirois commission reported and the conference of which I have been speaking took place. Since those days things have been humanized; we have cut down the institutionalism which seemed to exist in the minds of all those who had anything to do with dominion-provincial relations.
When I say to the Minister of Finance that I do not like the way the present arrangement has been made, it is because I do not think it will create any confidence at all among the provincial governments that this government intends to do what is right, or confidence that they will be able to get back into a conference and settle this matter on a basis of negotiation. But I am not overlooking the fact that the provinces who will receive the increases outlined in the paper which the minister has handed out to some of us today will be happy to have them. These increases are going to help them; there is no doubt about that. Moreover, this help is coming at a time when the provinces are facing a growing unemployment problem and conditions which, in some areas amounts almost to stagnation. As I say, these provinces are going to be very happy about what the government is doing.
I intend to support the proposal which has been made, and to show my good intentions in this regard I am not going to speak any longer, except to say this to the minister: make it abundantly clear to the provinces that you do intend to call a dominion- provincial conference as quickly as you can. And if you find that the hours of sitting are too long, then for goodness sake tell us that these hours will be shortened, and the rest of us will have a bit of a holiday watching you, and perhaps giving you a little bit of good advice on how to do it.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my friend the hon. member for Quebec East indicated in the speech he made, which raised the tone of debate in this house to the level to which we were accustomed before the present government took office and thereby heartened all of us on this side of the house, that he was not going to deal particularly with the grants to the Atlantic provinces but was going to consider primarily the general proposition of the increases to the provinces as a whole. It will not surprise you, Mr. Chairman, or any hon. member if I say that as a member from one of the constituencies in one of the Atlantic
Dominion-Provincial Relations provinces my main interest is in these grants to the Atlantic provinces. I may say at the outset that I do not think there is any doubt they will be warmly welcomed in all those provinces. There is absolutely no doubt that they are badly needed if the provincial services in those provinces are to be kept up to a level at all comparable with the services in any of the other provinces because even the Minister of National Revenue with all his pride in Nova Scotia which has without question the highest services of the four Atlantic provinces would admit they have not been able to keep pace in recent years even with the development of services in Saskatchewan where such services are the next lowest perhaps for reasons of distribution of income and that sort of thing.
I want to spend a few moments considering how this matter was dealt with in the conference in November. I will read briefly from what the Prime Minister said in his opening statement at that conference which I think puts the matter in the framework in which this proposal should be considered.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: From what page will you read?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I propose to read from page A-5 of the record of proceedings for Monday, November 25. The Prime Minister is reported as saying:
But I want to make this clear at the beginning. We are not placing before you any take it or leave it attitude; we are not taking any hard or fast position. We are not placing before you any rigid formulae.
It was surely not necessary to use the word "rigid" because there was no formula of any kind, rigid or flexible. I continue:
This conference was convened to seek your ideas and your proposals. Clearly we cannot expect to solve all our major problems in two days, but we can hope in that time to have a general survey of many of them.
I have a feeling, sir, that having had that general survey the Minister of Finance who made a speech that sounded like a cold shower of rain at the end of the opening session had had enough and right there on November 26 the Minister of Finance was determined that this conference would never meet again.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Such nonsense.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: The Minister of Finance can deny that if he likes but that is my opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: If I attempt to deny all the nonsense you utter I would be kept constantly busy at it.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I would now like to read from page B-l where the Prime Minister is reported as saying:
When we have your views and suggestions we want to study them in detail and prepare some

Dominion-Provincial Relations specific proposals to place before you at a mutually convenient time in the new year. This would be in accordance with the experience in one or other past conferences, and I believe it is the most acceptable procedure and the only feasible one under all the circumstances.
In other words the Prime Minister, unlike the Minister of Finance, admitted that that was the way it was done when we were in office. I stress these words:
-and I believe it is the most acceptable procedure and the only feasible one under all the circumstances.
Then on Saturday we had this diktat-and I spell the word for the benefit of Hansard. I think the Minister of Finance will understand. How does this compare with the attitude which was taken in the speech from the throne? Here are the words which the Prime Minister put in Her Majesty's mouth:
In domestic affairs my ministers look forward to meeting next month with the leaders of the provincial governments in order to discuss fiscal relations and to seek better understanding and arrangements of many aspects of our public finances.
Apparently they were seeking to achieve better understanding and better relations. Here is what the premier of Manitoba said about these better relations and the better understanding when he got the news on Saturday, as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press:
Campbell said on Saturday that although new offers will mean considerable extra revenue for Manitoba, he was disappointed in that it fell so far short of what Manitoba had proposed. He criticized the grants for not meeting the province's proposal for adopting a 15-15-50 formula-
I would remind the Minister of Finance that that was Mr. Frost's formula.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It was not Mr. Pickersgill's.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I continue:
-and for not being equalized to the yield in the highest province.
On the other hand he was glad to see the principle of equalization maintained for at least one year.
But Manitoba had expected something more permanent than a year-to-year basis, both from the point of view of equalization and "to the permanency of provincial revenues." "This means that Manitoba, along with the other less wealthy provinces, must continue to be extremely vigilant in seeing that the principle of equalization is not abandoned," he said. He feit that Manitoba deserved some of the credit that equalization had been maintained for a year at least.
I certainly agree with him. I think that Mr. Campbell and Mr. Douglas by the fight they put up at that conference, greatly assisted I am told in the later discussions by the premier of Alberta, preserved the principle of equalization which this government repeatedly refused under questioning in this house before the conference to say that it intended to maintain. I think this was retained
only because of the pressure brought to bear by those three premiers of the prairie provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Such utter nonsense.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Why did not the Minister of Finance get up in his place when he was asked about this? He had plenty of opportunity and so did the Prime Minister. They were asked over and over again if they were going to maintain the principle of equalization. I also asked the Minister of Public Works when he was leading the house and the Solicitor General was asked too. Of course the Solicitor General said the government was going to make the grants on an entirely different basis. The Minister of Finance can examine Hansard for October 18 and read what was said by the Solicitor General.
The fact of the matter is that this government did not know what it was going to do. It did not have the faintest idea. It would not even assure us that the principle of Mr. Harris and the principle of my right honourable friend-the principle of equalization- would be maintained. This principle has gone further in terms of giving a fair deal to people all across this country than has anything else that has been done in our domestic affairs since confederation. The government would not assure us that it would be continued until Mr. Campbell, Mr. Douglas and Mr. Manning and a number of the other premiers insisted upon it at that conference. The government finally realized there was no other way of doing it and knew that they did not dare abandon it.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Of course there was no agreement reached at the conference.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I do not think I said there was any agreement at the conference. Let me continue with what Mr. Campbell said as reported in the Winnipeg Free Press:
He was also "greatly concerned" over the government's method of dealing with this matter.
"The provinces were promised another conference," he said. "We counted on that to make additional representation and to have an opportunity of discussing the federal proposals, whatever they might be, rather than this method which seems to be not just a case of take it or leave it, as they called the former government's actions in this field, but the imposition upon us of a unilateral decree."
I agree with what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said on that matter. I agree also with what he said about a national principle. What is more, I think it can be shown from the record that these grants were not even originally intended to be available to all the Atlantic provinces. I think if hon. members will look at page C-3

of the record, where the Prime Minister is reported, they will see that he talked specifically about those Atlantic grants. This is what he said:
Now may I turn for a moment to the subject of fiscal relations in particular. As I view the situation, the first problem we have to consider is the need for some special recognition of the situation of the Atlantic provinces. There is, of course, a royal commission considering the particular problem of Newfoundland in accordance with the undertaking in the terms of union, so I shall not endeavour to express opinions upon Newfoundland's position pending receipt of the recommendations of the commission.
I believe that we all recognize, however, that the Atlantic provinces as a group are confronted with greater difficulties in public finance than the rest of the nation, if they are to maintain the sort of provincial and municipal services that Canadians generally expect. The taxable capacity of the Atlantic provinces, even in the best of times, is significantly lower than that of the other provinces.
Further down on page C-4 we find the following:
The dominion government and I believe the governments of the provinces recognize the special problem of the Atlantic provinces. My colleagues and I are prepared to recommend to parliament some form of special assistance to the governments of the Atlantic provinces. I ask you to consider what the total amount should be and how best it can be divided, for it must not be forgotten that this assistance will be provided by all the people of Canada.
That is what the Prime Minister had to say on this subject in his opening statement. I should like to read what the premier of Nova Scotia said on this subject at page K-4. It is quite brief. To make the context clear, Premier Stanfield had proposed what he called a maritime adjustment grant. He said:
I have referred to my proposal as a maritime adjustment grant but let me hasten to add that we in Nova Scotia are not unmindful of the financial difficulties of our sister province, Newfoundland. I felt, however, that in view of the fact that the report of the royal commission established to inquire into the position of Newfoundland relative to the maritime provinces is pending, it would be presumptuous for me to suggest a solution to Newfoundland's problems.
Mr. Flemming, the premier of New Brunswick, used almost precisely the same language at page N-5 of the record. Perhaps, so that there will be no dispute, I should read it too. He said:
You will note that in discussing the application of special adjustment grants I have not included the fiscal situation of Newfoundland. My reason for omitting to do so is obvious, since the financial position of that province is now the subject of inquiry by a royal commission.
On the following day, when the premier of Newfoundland spoke, he referred to this statement by the Prime Minister and to the
Dominion-Provincial Relations statements made by the two maritime premiers, which I have just quoted. Here is what Mr. Smallwood said at page FF-2 of the record for November 26:
Yesterday Premier Stanfield in his magnificent speech, and Premier Flemming in his magnificent speech, each had a paragraph of identical meaning referring to Newfoundland. You, Mr. Prime Minister, referred specifically to Newfoundland but in other terms, I am happy to say.
I got the impression from these two friends of mine that they are under the impression that so far as this conference is concerned Newfoundland might as well not be here, that our case is being taken care of by the royal commission. That is not so.
No matter what the royal commission recommends, no matter if they recommend the full amount we have asked for and if you and your colleagues recommend that amount to parliament and parliament passes it, all it will do will be to enable us, to enable the government of Newfoundland to continue the present levels and standards of our public services which are a quarter of a century behind the maritimes. That is all it can do at the most.
That is why I noted so carefully your words yesterday when you did not by any manner or means suggest that Newfoundland had no place in this conference today and yesterday. I thank you and Newfoundland thanks you for that.
Then, on page FF-4 we find the following:
We ask the Canadian government this simple question: Do you really think, does Canada think, does the parliament of Canada really think, does the Prime Minister think that Canada has done its full duty to the new province when it implements the recommendations of the royal commission which will enable it to maintain our present levels and standards?
Is that all? Are we not to be invited to future fiscal conferences? Does that settle Newfoundland's case, just the implementing of the report of the royal commission? Are we not part of this fiscal conference when the Prime Minister said yesterday that he will recommend to parliament some additional and special consideration for the Atlantic provinces? In adopting the new term "the Atlantic provinces" did he not include Newfoundland? I am sure he did. Was that not something separate and apart altogether from the royal commission? Surely the recommendations of the royal commission have nothing to do with this fiscal conference, nothing whatever.
1 was very pleased when the Minister of Finance said today that he agreed with that view expressed by Mr. Smallwood. I can assure the minister-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: There never was any question about it.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: There are not many occasions when I have agreed with the minister during this session but I can assure him that those words of his will be appreciated in Newfoundland and will be remembered.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It is a good thing that something will be.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have one further quotation to read from the record and it is from

Dominion-Provincial Relations the Prime Minister's statement in reply to Mr. Smallwood and is found at page FF-7. It reads as follows:

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I will say no more at this time, hut I would point out to the premier of Newfoundland that when I used the expression "the Atlantic provinces" I anticipated what his views would be in regard to the use of that expression.
I have read these extracts into the record for two reasons. The first is, it was quite apparent that there was a misunderstanding on the part of the premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick as to the real purpose of the royal commission which is now considering term 29 of the terms of union, and that misunderstanding has been cleared up. I do feel, sir, that there was some doubt when this conference met that it was intended to include Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: There was never any doubt.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
It was the insistence of
the premier of Newfoundland that resolved the doubt when the conference was over.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Oh, no. There never was
any question about it at any time.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I ask the minister to read
very carefully the very ambiguous language used by the Prime Minister at the beginning, which I read from the record.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: There is nothing ambiguous about it.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
If the minister says that
there never was any doubt about it I accept his word and we need not debate it any further.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman read into the record the unambiguous remark of Mr. Smallwood in October or November of 1955 that he was not interested in the conference; that he was depending on the recommendations of the royal commission? Will he read that into the record?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I have read the record of the November conference extremely carefully. I listened to almost every word that was spoken there. I have read over every word since, and I could not find any such statement by Mr. Smallwood. If the hon. gentleman can, he will have an opportunity in this debate to put it on the record.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I will put it on the record.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I would be very interested indeed to see it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: I said November, but I meant October.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman is referring to something that happened at some

other time, then that is different. I was referring to the November conference.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: No, the one before that.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I know to what the hon. gentleman is referring if he is referring to October 1955. I heard Mr. Smallwood's speech there and I remember very well what it was. He indicated that so far as general fiscal arrangements were concerned he thought the premiers of the other provinces, which had been provinces for years and years, could put up a better case than he could, and that if he got what they got that would be all right so far as the general share was concerned. However, what Newfoundland was primarily interested in was this royal commission on the revision of terms. I recall that very well. I think it was a very reasonable position for Mr. Smallwood to take.
I might remind the Minister of National Revenue that at that conference Nova Scotia was represented by Mr. Hicks, who was then premier. This brings me to the point I had intended to make anyway, that it was Mr. Hicks who, not in October but in April 1955, originated this idea of a special fiscal grant to the Atlantic provinces and to whom credit should go for that idea. If hon. members would look at the proceedings of the preliminary meeting of the federal-provincial conference for 1955 in Ottawa on April 26, 1955, pages 26 and 27-I am not going to read this whole record because it is somewhat lengthy-they would see that Mr. Hicks set out a formula which I might say, as a Liberal I am proud to say, was capable of national application to every province of Canada.
I think every member in this chamber from the Atlantic provinces, no matter to which party he belongs, appreciates the fact that these special grants are being made. I think all of us appreciate the attitude that was taken by the other provincial premiers. I think all of us appreciate the attitude that so far has been taken in the debate in this house, and which I expect will continue to be taken in the debate. I do believe that there is a much healthier attitude amongst all Canadians toward the Atlantic region than there has ever been before since confederation. Hon. members will not agree entirely with this statement and may think I am a little biased in making it, but I do believe that when my right hon. friend was successful in bringing Newfoundland into Canada it did attract a new attention, a new interest and a new pride in Canadians all over the country in that part of Canada. In these last 10 years there has been a much greater interest in and understanding of the Atlantic

region than there has ever been before. Certainly in these last 10 years there has been a great deal more done for that region than ever was done before.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: My hon. friend would not expect the province to receive payment twice, would he? maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I fully understand the minister's explanation. However, may I point out to the minister that on the front page of the Vancouver Sun of Saturday January 25, the headline reads "$5.5 million for B.C. in New Tax Grants" and underneath that "More Promised for Hospitals". This afternoon we find out that instead of getting $5,563,000 more under the new legislation that is proposed, we shall be getting only $2,842,000 more. That is a considerable difference, having regard to what we were on Saturday assuming that we would get. The amount of $2,842,000 is only one per cent of the budget of our government in British Columbia, and it is not very much to write home about. Unfortunately for me, however, I had already written home. I had already advised the weekly newspapers at home that the federal government had finally moved and that this year our provincial coffers could expect to be enriched by over $5 million. I shall now be obliged to report to those same newspapers that the impression left by the minister's announcement was an erroneous one.
I realize that hon. members from the Atlantic provinces are not going to look a gift horse in the mouth and that therefore they may not be too severely critical of the method by which this money is going to be given to them. I am referring now to the special grants that were announced for the Atlantic provinces totalling some $25 million. Maybe if I were a member from that area, I also would wait and see.
However, I think we in this group are able to say that while we are in hearty agreement with more money being supplied to the Atlantic provinces, we do not like the

manner in which it is being given. We do not think it ought to be given as a gift. We think it ought not to be a donation because it puts a political weapon in the hands of the government in office in Ottawa in that the people of the province can then be subjected to pressure or can be influenced as to how they will vote according to the degree to which the parties promise to raise, lower or abolish these grants.
We believe that a formula should have been arrived at whereby these people would have received this additional money as of right. We feel that in their contribution to the development of Canada over the years long before our western provinces were formed the people in the Atlantic provinces were exhausting their energies on behalf of the development of the then unsettled parts of Canada. We feel that they have a fair claim and that they should not be regarded as poor relations.
As I look over the resolution and as I think of its effect in terms of the money payments that were announced, I have the feeling that here is a part of the pay-off of the last election. I agree that a fair measure of justice is being done to individual taxpayers in the powerful province of Quebec. All of those individual taxpayers there will receive some of the benefits. To some extent at least the burden of double taxation for them will have been removed. However, when I look at the amount of money that the province of Ontario is to receive, in relation to that received by other provinces, I cannot help but feel that this is part of the compensation that is being offered for the help that the premier of that province gave to the Conservatives in the last federal election.
In the forthcoming appeal to the electorate I mean to commend this government for many things that it has been able to do for the Canadian people. At the same time I also mean to condemn them as roundly as I can for some of the major pledges which they gave but which as yet they have not yet seen fit to implement. The major pledge to which I am now specifically referring is the one to relieve the ever-growing burden on our municipalities. I greatly regret the fact that this new arrangement does nothing to relieve the burden on our municipal governments. I should like to read into the record only a few sentences of what was said on other occasions when the problem of taxation at various levels of government was before the house. The Minister without Portfolio, the hon. member for Greenwood, had this to say as recorded at page 4786 of Hansard of May 17, 1954:
It is no answer to shrug off the municipalities. With all due deference, I think the Minister of 96698-2451
Dominion-Provincial Relations Finance (Mr. Abbott) is inclined to do that. The municipalities are greatly handicapped in obtaining any new revenue. Real estate has to bear practically the whole load. Real estate raises 85 per cent of municipal taxes, and it is a burden which becomes heavier and heavier.
The Minister of Finance, who was then the member for Eglinton, had this to say on the same day as reported on page 4788 of Hansard:
The federal government, with its abundant sources, should be devising ways of helping the municipalities to meet these urgent demands for necessary but costly services which they are financially unable to provide.
And on page 4789, he said:
There must be, in my submission, an opening of the eyes of the federal government to the way in which they are increasing the burdens and the difficulties of the municipalities.
We have been attempting over a number of months now to see whether the eyes of the new Minister of Finance were open to the needs of the municipalities. In the terms of the resolution he has introduced to this house and in the explanations he has given he is as blind to the needs of the municipalities as any former minister of finance has been.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: What rot!

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The minister feels that no commitment was made in the heat of the election campaign, but I would refer him to an item appearing in Moody Advance in the month of May, 1957, in which my Conservative opponent in the last election is reported as follows:
She also contended that property taxes will continue to rise unless the federal government increases grants to municipalities, and advocated the abolition of sales and excise taxes on municipal and school board purchases.
On practically every platform on which the kind lady Alderman Jane Kilmer appeared she appealed to the people to vote Conservative because that would mean more money for the municipalities. She was a fine candidate and indeed I regret that the ruthlessness of party politics in the Conservative party made it necessary for the convention not to do her the honour of renominating her. They felt a man might be more able to gain the riding.
I have here the political education program put out by the Canadian Labour Congress. It talks of the union vote and lists all the promises which the Conservatives made in the last election. Under provincial-federal tax payment arrangements, Item (1) is:
Provide more equitable share of tax yields to the provinces and municipalities.
The resolution introduced by the minister makes no allowance for the needs of municipalities. I also notice in the blue pamphlet upon which the picture of the Prime Minister

Dominion-Provincial Relations appears, and which was so widely used in the last election, the statement is made that out of every dollar of taxes paid by the Canadian people the federal government is collecting 76 per cent, the provincial governments 10 per cent and the municipal governments 14 per cent. One would imagine that once elected to office these people would do something serious about rearranging tax receipts.
We went to some lengths at the opening of this session to impress upon this government the need for municipal representation at the last dominion-provincial conference. I am fully aware of the constitutional complications there. However, a feeling exists- and I think there is some justification for it -that this government has made up its mind that it is going to make a bit more money available to the provincial governments here and there across Canada and it is then going to say, "Well, the municipalities after all are the responsibility of the provincial governments; we have helped the provincial governments and it is now up to them to help the municipal governments."
I am afraid that is not going to be satisfactory. Some of the provincial governments are simply not able, even with more money from the federal treasury, to enable municipalities to meet their obligations. The taxes on our homes are rising year by year and they will continue to rise unless some action is taken. I do not blame local municipal councils for adding to the tax burdens on our homes; it is the only way they can raise the money to pay the ever-increasing expenses which they have to pay. They have no more power to cease and desist from adding to the tax burden on homes than we have to stop the tides of the sea. I have in my hand a letter dated January 14, 1958, written by the new reeve of the municipality of Burnaby, in which he says, among other things:
This would be as good a time as any to inform you that a good deal of concern is being shown on the part of the ratepayers of Burnaby over the matter of local taxation. You will appreciate that those people of limited and fixed income find upward revision of their municipal taxes extremely difficult to bear. Unfortunately, statutes governing the scope of the municipalities prevent them from making suitable tax adjustments in favour of these people.
I have advocated in this house as far back as April 26, 1954 the establishment of a permanent dominion-provincial secretariat. If we had such a secretariat we would find our conferences between the provincial premiers and the government in Ottawa to be much more fruitful. I am pleased to see that the premier of Saskatchewan at the April meeting of 1955 endorsed, at least the principle of the establishment of a secretariat at

which there would be a continuing review of the problems brought about by our federal system of government.
We have had for years as the first item in our British Columbia C.C.F. program the establishment of a dominion-provincial secretariat. The minister emphasized a little while ago "We respect the constitution", but may I say there is not a single one of the four national political parties which could not say the same thing and could not say it with equal emphasis. Any political movement which wants to be national in scope must have a healthy respect for the constitution. I would, however, like at this time to propose a number of methods by which the financial burden of our municipalities might have been eased by this government, if the minister, in his announcement, had seen fit to do so.
First of all I would advocate, along with many other people in Canada who have made representations in this respect, that the federal government immediately cease and desist from collecting sales tax on anything purchased for local, municipal, school or hospital authorities. That, in itself, would go a considerable distance. I recognize at once that the former government amended this legislation, in some degree removing the burden from municipal offices in this respect. However, there still remains a considerable sales tax collected from local government bodies.
I should like also to recommend that this new government now accept the theory that crown property should be taxed for municipal purposes in the same way as is any other property. I know the previous government made some improvements in this respect, but in the field of assessment crown properties still do not pay their fair share of municipal taxation.
Another means by which this government could do considerably more to ease the burden on other levels of government, both provincial and municipal, would be to adopt a more generous policy with regard to its contribution toward highways and all manner of roads. In 1954 I proposed-and I will offer this suggestion again to the new government, hoping it will fall on ears that are not so deaf-that the federal government should assume all responsibility for a major national highway network, and that the provincial government should be left with the responsibility for only secondary highways, with municipal governments responsible only for access roads. That would go much further than the present proposal put forward by the minister in easing the tax burden on lower levels of government.
I welcome the announcement of the Minister of National Health and Welfare the

other day with regard to increased grants for hospital construction. I think the government might have gone further still. After all, even under the new arrangement they are paying only about $2,000 of about $20,000, which is the cost of a bed in the Vancouver general hospital. In other words, this is only about 10 per cent of the cost. The federal government could very well assume a larger share and thus relieve both provincial and municipal governments of a considerable burden.
If the federal government will introduce a national health plan, all inclusive, and including medical care, they would relieve provincial and municipal governments of the heavy cost of paying for health services for welfare cases, and also relieve municipalities of the per diem levy which they have to pay, at least in the province from which I come.
If the federal government wished to show practical sympathy for the needs of the provinces it might consider more than removing the floor with regard to when they begin paying part of the cost of the care of the employable unemployed. The federal government should now implement the proposal contained in the green book of 1945 in which the late Mr. Mackenzie King offered on behalf of the federal government to assume full responsibility for looking after the employable unemployed throughout the nation.
Possibly one of the most useful manners in which this government could extend help to the lower levels of government would be to reactivate the Municipal Improvements Assistance Act. On a number of occasions in the last several months we have asked the minister whether it is the intention of the government to reactivate this measure. The hon. member for Dauphin spoke at length on this, as recorded on pages 95 to 97 of Hansard, and a number of other hon. members have referred to it on various occasions. However, the answer I myself received from the minister was that this, obviously, would be a matter of government policy. And he gave a similar answer to each of us who asked about it.
I realize that this is a matter of government policy, and it is government policy that we are speaking of now. This one move, if it had been made, would have been more welcome among the people back home than the announcement the minister has made. The record of this act has been an excellent one. It operated from 1938 to 1940. I believe 110 loans were made. Money was made available to municipalities at a low rate of interest, and every single cent was repaid; the federal treasury did not lose a penny. The act was a means of providing employment to thousands of Canadians, and it could do the same
Dominion-Provincial Relations today. It enabled many municipalities to build waterworks, sewers and the like, and our municipalities have asked me to ask the government as often as I can to make this act operative again.
The federal government could help the lower levels of government-I should not call them "lower" because in many ways they are the higher levels of government-by amending the National Housing Act. Municipal councils are anxious to make serviced lots available to would-be homeowners, but they have not the necessary money with which to undertake the work.
The federal government could have done much to relieve anxiety throughout Canada by agreeing to sit down with the provinces and explore ways and means of aiding them in the provision of educational facilities. If the federal government would agree to assist the provinces and, through them, the school boards in the building of schools, that alone would mean in my own province far more than does the present offer of the federal government to rearrange the formula under the tax sharing agreement.
I suspect that the Conservative party believes in the reallocation of taxation powers. I think the present economic situation in Canada should lead to a reconsideration of that old approach. We have always opposed the reallocation of the powers of taxation. We think that the federal government must continue to have these powers in order to ensure the economic welfare of the nation, and that it needs the power of taxation in order to carry out this task effectively. However, we believe that the federal government should then, without violating the principles of our constitution, do everything in its power to relieve those who are doing their utmost to make democracy work back home.
I should like at this time to pay tribute to the many thousands of Canadians who are volunteering their services, many of them without any remuneration whatsoever, and who are the bulwark of Canadian democracy. I refer to members of hospital boards, school boards and municipal councils at home. I know that we in our ivory tower here-or is it a granite tower?-come to think of ourselves before much time is passed as the symbols of democracy. We are nothing of the kind; if anything we are sometimes in the public mind symbols of arrogance and symbols of a government far removed from the people it professes to serve. Democracy is built from the bottom up, and if we continue to ignore the needs of the people who are working at home to make our system work and to provide our people with their social needs, we are going to suffer the consequences and

Dominion-Provincial Relations create a feeling of cynicism among our people of which there is already far too much.
Mr. Chairman, I have spoken today because taxes on our homes are increasing and they will continue to go up until we decide to declare a halt to further increases of taxes on the homes of our people.

The Minister of Finance when he spoke earlier this afternoon said that the members of his party had opposed the tax agreements made in 1956 because they were inadequate. I think perhaps that may be a faithful description of the attitude which the hon. member himself took during the debate on the legislation which we were then considering but it certainly does not accurately describes the reasons given by his colleagues in the Conservative party at that time for the stand which they then took both at the resolution stage and on the second reading of the very resolution which it is proposed to amend by the bill to follow this present resolution.
I should like to put on Hansard a few excerpts from the remarks made by hon. members of the Conservative party who did not seem then to have at all the same ideas they must now have in order to bring forward for consideration of this committee the resolution which is now under discussion. The then leader of the opposition Mr. Drew, in 1956, as recorded at page 5993 of Hansard, said-

The subject now before us is whether we really believe in the federal system sufficiently to do our utmost at this time to find real agreement with the provincial governments and with the municipalities which are very real entities indeed as to the allocation of taxes which will make it possible for them to carry out the heavy responsibilities which they cannot ignore and cannot shirk.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, this was the lead for the other members of the party to insist upon a re-allocation of the powers of taxation. The present Minister of National Revenue followed the same line of argument
[Mr. Regier.l

and I should like to quote three phrases from his remarks, the first as recorded at page 6015 of Hansard:
We in this party believe and have said time and again that there should be a re-allocation of responsibilities, that there should be a re-allocation of taxation powers-
That is only part of the phrase but what I have omitted does not change its sense. On the following page of Hansard, page 6016, he is reported as saying:
There certainly is something wrong with the principle suggested by the government in this resolution.
This is the very principle which the Minister of National Revenue is supporting today in the resolution which is now before the committee because if he did not support the resolution which we are now considering it would not be before the committee. On page 6017 he is reported as having said:
But a formula should be worked out that would recognize the capacity to pay of the individual as well as the number of heads in a province.
At least so far as that part of his remarks is concerned it seems now to be translated into something more than mere words which I am afraid is the assessment that one should place upon his other remarks.
The present Solicitor General also took part in the discussion and I am quoting from the translation of his remarks to be found at page 6031 of Hansard:
What is in fact required is a federal-provincial conference in which the federal government and the provinces will consider the steps to be taken for a fair distribution of taxation fields, so that the provinces may play their part in their own sphere.
The present Minister of Trade and Commerce also entered the debate and as recorded at page 6064 said:
But the rest of the matter has not been attacked, and that is the division of responsibility between the dominion government and the provincial jurisdictions.
Apparently he felt it was not enough to say it once for he said it again as recorded at page 6065:
-surely the present approach should be toward an investigation of the division of responsibility as between the dominion and provincial authorities.
Twice was not enough; we had it a third time as recorded at page 6066 when he said:
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that a dominion-provincial conference be called devoted to the task of solving the division of responsibilities as between the dominion and provincial governments.
The present Minister of Justice entered the debate, too, and as recorded at page 6335 said:
I am putting this forward as a serious proposal, that what is needed, rather than trying to force our relationships into this pre-tailored fiscal garment, is a meeting of all the governments with a view to assessing their needs and what if any

exchange of constitutional responsibilities can be arranged by mutual consent. Then having reached agreement on this point, arrange a federal-provincial fiscal program which will enable the various governments to discharge their agreed responsibilities.
The interesting fact is that so many members of the present cabinet were strong advocates of this idea of a re-allocation of taxation powers between the dominion government and the provincial governments and yet at the very first opportunity they had of following up these ideas which they had preached so assiduously in the past when they were sitting in the opposition benches they backed away from the step entirely. I think it has been the general experience of people who have been interested in this field of dominion-provincial relations in the matter of taxes that there has been a large body of criticism emanating from members of the Conservative party both provincial and federal advocating not an extension of the present scheme of tax sharing but a formal redistribution of taxation powers. However, their arguments are of the hit and run type. They enunciate the principle and then back away from spelling out how they would propose to carry it out.
I notice that in the present instance the government convened a conference with the provinces in November and yet nowhere on the record of the public deliberations does one find anything which suggests that this proposal was put forward by the present government as a matter for discussion with the provinces. Surely no one would suggest that there was anything to prevent the government from carrying out the idea which it advocated so extensively in the past.
I would now like to quote some comments made by the Solicitor General as recently as the present session. They are indeed interesting when one realizes what the Minister of Finance is now asking this committee to do, to extend further the principle of the present tax-sharing agreements. Note the words of the Solicitor General in answer to a question put to him as found on page 129 of Hansard of October 18, 1957:
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I would like to tell my honourable friend that I am still opposed to subsidies such as were proposed by the former government. As to his question, it seems to be a hypothetical one, but I am ...
At this point there was an interruption; then he went on:
. .. and a political one, yes. I want to tell him that the proposals of the federal government are not yet known, but I am convinced that they will be made on a very different basis than those of the former government.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
(Text):
I cannot resist the temptation to translate this for the benefit of members sitting on the government benches. The Solicitor General said in effect, "I want to tell you that the proposals of the federal government are not yet known. I am convinced they were made on a very different basis from those of the former government." Therefore, we see that although the very proposals which are being implemented in this resolution are very different in the mind of the Solicitor General from those which served as a basis of the present fiscal agreements, here we find the Solicitor General, as a member of the government, supporting the very proposals which he criticized in no uncertain terms on the day that I referred to a moment ago.
Then, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word about the conference which was held in November. I could not help feeling some amusement when I read the words of the present Prime Minister as reported at page 6369 of Hansard for 1956, and I do not doubt but hon. gentlemen opposite will take certain amusement also from hearing them. He said:
I wonder often why this government has not taken the provinces into its confidence.
Is that not a strange statement when we consider the action taken by the Prime Minister himself last Friday night in acquainting the provinces for the first time of a purely unilateral decision of this government as to what it was going to do as to the payments of 1958-59? The Prime Minister went on:
Why these short-term meetings:	why these
gatherings of a day or two?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Who is this talking?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
This is the Prime Minister speaking, who complained of the shortness of duration of those conferences in past times. He said:
Why these gatherings of a day or two? Why do we not have a meeting of the federal authorities, the provincial authorities and the municipalities?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister had in mind that the municipalities should be present but now, unfortunately, he has found that there were constitutional difficulties in the way in the year 1957 that did not seem to be present at all in 1956. I continue:
Call it a constitutional convention, if you like, without the power of amendment of the constitution in respect of those fundamental rights which are inherent in the constitution, but why not have a gathering designed to bring about the reconsideration of a problem which for the last 13 years or so has become increasingly complex?
I quote these words, Mr. Chairman, and everybody will realize how apt they are and the extent to which they apply to the conference which was held in November, and the action which the Prime Minister took last

Dominion-Provincial Relations Friday night in informing the provincial governments of the decision taken by the present government. Listen to what the Solicitor General had to say, as reported at page 6028 of Hansard, and this is a translation, Mr. Chairman:
In fact, the resolution moved by the Honourable Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and upon which we are called upon to pass judgment, is not the result of a conference between the federal government and the provinces; not at all.
And yet this very resolution, Mr. Chairman, which we are being asked to pass is not the result of a conference between the federal government and the provinces. Let us make no mistake about that. This is a purely unilateral action on the part of gentlemen on the treasury benches. I continue with the quotation from the Solicitor General:
We are not being asked to ratify an agreement between the dominion government and the provinces, an agreement reached following long negotiations where every party concerned had previously examined the proposals made. On the contrary, once again the federal government acted in a centralizing and unilateral way.
How aptly these words of the Solicitor General apply to the actions of the government of which he is one of the members. He continued:
It called the provinces together, read its proposal and asked them what they thought about it, made a few minor changes here and there and said: "Do as you wish; this is as far as we can go," knowing full well that the provinces are not in a position to do without them, even though they found the amounts altogether inadequate.
In this particular case the government did not even call the provinces together to acquaint them of this decision with regard to these additional payments; they advised them merely by telephone. Mr. Chairman, I hope the Solicitor General will reread the words which he used when he was sitting on this side of the house. But one cannot avoid the reflection that there are merely 20 feet of green carpet which seems to separate those benches from which I speak and the treasury benches. By merely crossing that carpet the hon. gentlemen who are Minister of National Revenue, Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Solicitor General have all undergone extraordinary transformations in their thinking. They no longer think the way they did when they were on this side of the house. They have a new formula which is different from what they had in 1956. By merely crossing this 20 feet of green carpet they have suddenly attained a virtue that they did not have in 1956. The Minister of National Revenue laughs. He occasionally used to do that when he was on this side of the house, therefore in that respect he has not changed by moving across these 20 feet of green carpet.
I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

speechtext:
Perhaps this will be my last word on the subject. It does not often happen that the reality of Conservative promises is greater than the promises themselves.
The next point with which I want to deal is the fact that throughout the election campaign the Prime Minister was making promises of one kind or another. I am only going to touch on two or three. One was to increase old age security and other social allowances; the second was the reduction in taxes, and the third quite positively was an increase in the benefits of tax sharing with the various provincial governments. I am not going into the numerous statements that the Prime Minister made on the subject of the increased revenues to the provinces. All I want to do is stress the fact that as the campaign went on many Canadians began to wonder how all this was going to be accomplished within the limits of the available resources.
When the present Prime Minister reached Saskatoon on May 27 he held a press conference. He was asked specifically how all of these promises fitted in with the available revenues. I am quoting from a Canadian Press report in the Montreal Gazette, May 28, 1957, and I will just quote two paragraphs from it:
He-
That is of course the Prime Minister.
-was asked how his party's policy involving increased expenditures squares with the promise to reduce unnecessary taxation.
Mr. Diefenbaker replied that both could be done without a budget deficit. His estimate had been made on the basis of steadily increasing budget surplus.
He went on to say:
The surplus last year was $500 million and if economic forecast of trade minister Howe was correct the surplus in the current fiscal year would be 50 per cent greater.
The significant phrase, Mr. Chairman, is that all this was to be done on the basis of a balanced budget. We have not had any kind of national accounting that would enable us to determine in complete detail to what extent there has been departure from the so-called balanced budget. We have had some figures that the Minister of Finance himself has given us after some rather limited observations of his own on the subject. From time to time, as various additional measures involving increased expenditures have come before us, we have been told what the overall
3876	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations cost would be. I want, in the few minutes that remain, just to put on Hansard the overall picture that results from what the present government has done since it has been in office, and the effects on next year's revenue of what was done at the earlier session in
1957.	Because of the limitation of time, I shall have to try to put it in very compressed form.
So far as expenditures are concerned, the first item will be an increase in the year 1958-59, the next fiscal year, over the expenditure of 1957-58 for social security payments and veterans' benefits. In respect of the increases made by the Liberal government, the additional cost next year will be $40 million and in respect of those made by the present government, $65.9 million, making a total of $115.9 million.
Then, as the Minister of National Health and Welfare has told us, the increased cost for 1958-59 over the current year of unemployment assistance to the provinces will be $11.9 million. Perhaps I should say that is the inference to be drawn from these figures. Then we shall have next year to pay 12 months of pay and allowances at the present increased level instead of 11 months. That will amount to another $8.3 million.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has told us that the national hospital plan will come into effect on July 1 of this year for three or four or perhaps even more provinces. I take it that we may infer that, as far as Ontario is concerned, it will come into effect on January 1, 1959. So far as I can make out from the available information, that will add $60 million to the expenditures for next year.
Then the other day-I think it was Saturday-the same minister announced increases in the grants to be made under the national health plan. I find it difficult to estimate the cost but I think it is probably a conservative estimate to say that the additional cost next year would probably be at least $3.5 million. Then this resolution that we are discussing at the moment will add $87.2 million to the expenditures. That makes a total addition to the expenditures of $285.8 million.
At the earlier session of 1957 reductions in taxes were made, the full effect of which will only be felt next year; but it was estimated that the additional cost next year was $73 million. So far as the reductions recommended by the present Minister of Finance are concerned, that is another $152 million. In addition to that, he has referred to the legislation to replace the Dominion Succession Duty Act which will further reduce revenues by $8 million. Hence we have reductions in revenue in prospect for 1958-59


of $233 million. If we add that amount to the additional expenditures to which I referred a moment ago we find that the change in the balance of the budget for next year is $518.8 million.
From that figure we must obviously deduct the amount paid in the current year to the Canada Council, namely $100 million, thus bringing the prospective difference between this year's budget and last year's budget to an amount of $418.8 million. The minister told us that he expected to have a surplus for the current year of $80 million. Let us take that amount into account also and deduct it. Thus we see that with the arrangement which we are discussing at the moment we have a deficit in prospect for next year of $338.8 million. That does not take account of the fact that through the natural increase in number, both of persons drawing old age security and those drawing family allowances, there will be a further addition to the social security bill next year of some $33.8 million.
Assuming that the payments that are provided for in this resolution are made, we therefore see in prospect for next year a deficit of $375 million in round figures whereas the Prime Minister told us and told the electors of Canada all across the country in the spring of 1957 that all of this was to be done on a balanced budget. We have the opportunity today of seeing just how unbalanced the budget is. Of course, to encourage the Minister of Finance, perhaps, we have the statement which his colleague the Minister of Justice made in 1956 in which, as reported at page 6336 of Hansard, he said:
It is true that that suggestion was made and is still made by the Conservative opposition, that if this government really put its mind to it, it could save upward of $500 million without reducing essential expenditures.
No doubt the Minister of Finance will consult with his colleague the Minister of Justice to discover the secret of where this $500 million can be lopped off the national budget without affecting essential expenditures. But I have an idea that even the idea of the Minister of Justice with respect to those reductions has undergone a transformation since he moved from this side of the house to the other side.
The Minister of Finance himself this afternoon said that no increase in taxes was involved in this operation. If he really believes that, I think he is deluding himself. However, I am sure he is not deluding the taxpayers of Canada because the fact remains that it is impossible to pay out $87.2 million to the provinces, no matter how worthy are the purposes, without affecting the taxpayers' tax bill. I must admit to a feeling of some

disquiet when I see the additions to expenditures and the subtractions from revenue that I just mentioned a moment ago. It seems to me that it puts the government in a rather unhappy position. I take it that next year it will want to increase the volume of capital expenditures. It certainly ought to be thinking in those terms.
The minister himself has led the taxpayers to believe-and he did so after presenting his budget, if it can be so called, earlier in December-that his party was not satisfied that it had given all the tax reductions which it had hoped to give. I hope the taxpayers will not be expecting too much of my hon. friends opposite. With the unbalance that he and his government have brought about already I think he is going to be hard put to do much more in the way of tax reduction than he has already done. I note that the newspapers are already referring to the reduction as insignificant. I am sure that he does not feel that they are insignificant but it will give him an idea of how the taxpayers are already feeling about something he did last December. I feel perfectly sure that, with the beginning of the year-of course nothing would be further from his mind than to make reductions in taxes on the eve of an election, because he criticized that procedure so frequently in the past and I know he would not want to do something now that he criticized in the past-he will have his work cut out for him. I may tell him that I am going to watch with real interest the measures he takes to bring this budget back out of the unbalance which this government has put it into.
