speechtext:
The Minister of Finance,
on July 23, 1956 said, as recorded at page 6296 of Hansard:
There is no use so far as Her Majesty's loyal opposition is concerned, asking us to approve a form of dominion-provincial fiscal arrangement which has not received the approval of a single provincial government. If there could be, on the part of the federal government, a change in attitude, and after that change in attitude they will call a new conference, then fruitful results I am certain could be achieved.
I would think the Minister of Finance should have made some effort to find out from the provincial premiers what their reaction was. We all sympathize with Premier Bennett of British Columbia who read in the papers on Saturday that British Columbia would receive $5.5 million and then he read in today's paper that owing to a mistake of the Minister of Finance or the Prime Minister this amount would be slashed to $2.8
3878	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations million, a loss of $2J million. This is a very serious matter for any province in these very difficult days of financing.
It is now 21 years since this controversial question of dominion-provincial relations received the attention of the lay makers of Canada. I have read the report on dominion-provincial relations, books 1, 2 and 3. The member for Quebec East was associated with this very important commission but world war II interrupted the discussions which would have during the forties ironed out some of these problems. In that report I find some references at which we should look very carefully.
It seems very clear that we appear to be in another depression, which so far as agriculture is concerned is as serious a depression as that of the thirties. On page 150 I read that the disparities in incidence of depression on different regions had the effect of a loss of income which was most severe in western Canada and that the declines ranged from 72 per cent in Saskatchewan to 36 per cent in Nova Scotia. The average per capita income in the various provinces across Canada from 1928 to 1929 and then to 1933 is shown as a reduction in my province of 72 per cent whereas in the province of Nova Scotia we find the percentage decrease is down to 36 per cent. There is another reference in the report to the fact that the people of Saskatchewan had suffered a reduction in income during the previous decade which had probably been unparalleled in peacetime in any other civilized country; net agricultural income averaging some $200 million a year in the late twenties are reported to have fallen to an actual negative amount in 1931 and 1932 and was only about one-tenth of that average in 1937.
There were some very useful recommendations, one of which was that the dominion should assume full responsibility for unemployed employables and in certain eventualities offer to relieve primary industries with certain jurisdictional changes which might be necessary, which should be made to enable the dominion government to fulfil this responsibility. There is also a very interesting section on municipal finances and the report remarks that a great many changes have taken place since confederation. At that time the responsibilities of the municipal authorities could be attended to without large disbursements, but 21 years ago, as now, the municipal authorities in Canada were confronted with responsibilities which they could not meet from their available tax revenues.
The other day in discussing another matter I referred to a municipality which is partly in Mackenzie constituency and partly in the 

Prime Minister's constituency. I know of another municipality in Mackenzie where the reeve is the Conservative candidate who is running in the next election and the candidate who ran in the last election. He is a very able citizen who is doing his very best to manage the affairs of the municipality. Now the arrears in the last five years have gone from $21,000 to $27,000, $39,000, $54,000 and, in 1956, $54,400.
I am sure it is not because the reeve of that municipality is not efficient and it is not because he is a Conservative while the government of Saskatchewan is C.C.F. The reason for these arrears mounting like a snowball is because the taxpayers in the municipality are unable to meet their costs of production and all their expenses. I have in my hand a list of the arrears for one of the school units which is also partly in the Prime Minister's constituency and partly in my own constituency of Mackenzie. I refer to the school unit of Nipawin. The amounts due to this school unit from the municipalities in that area have gone up from $272,000 to $396,000, $497,000 and $545,000 in the last few years.
As I have indicated, we are in the midst of a depression which in many respects is more serious than the depression of the thirties. There was never a time in the history of Canada when a bushel of wheat would buy so little. Farm marketings of wheat have been poor; in fact the problems are not caused by the municipal authorities but by the fact that the farmers are unable to sell their wheat because we are losing our markets. As a result, many of these municipalities have had to go into debt to the banks to such an extent that they do not know how they can continue.
The Wheat Review for December, 1957, published by the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, says that deliveries of wheat by farmers in the three prairie provinces up to December 18 of the current crop year have amounted to 103.7 million bushels, representing a decline of 15 per cent from the total of 122.5 million marketed during the corresponding period of 1956 and sharply below the ten year average marketings for the period of 191.3 million bushels. So when, as a result of federal fiscal and export trade policies, farm marketings are reduced to the extent I have indicated our municipal authorities are in real difficulties.
I am sure that most of the members have read with a good deal of interest the letter written to the Prime Minister on December 18 by the premier of Manitoba in connection with this important subject. Premier Campbell has had an acknowledgment from the

Dominion-Provincial Relations
Prime Minister that the letter was received and I know that the Prime Minister was in Winnipeg over the weekend and probably had a chance to have a verbal discussion but, so far as this House of Commons is concerned, we have no information as to what the Prime Minister has put in a letter to Mr. Campbell. Premier Campbell remarks that it was at the federal insistance that the conference found itself having to deal with two or three specific matters, including the so-called Atlantic provinces adjustment, before the meeting broke up. He says that it would appear to the Manitoba representatives that the Prime Minister and his ministers were unwilling or unable to deal with the broader question of the general financial arrangements between the federal and provincial governments.
As my colleague from Winnipeg North Centre pointed out this afternoon, it is nonsense to suggest that a conference could not have been held while parliament was in session. In view of the statements made by members of the present cabinet two years ago when this matter was before parliament I should have thought that an effort would have been made to work out some formula which would have satisfied the premiers of the provinces.
Mr. Campbell said in his letter:
We also emphasized the point that adverse weather conditions or other unfavourable circumstances might place one or all of the prairie provinces in the same position and consequently that the policy should not be termed an Atlantic adjustment . . .
I have already indicated the extent of the crisis which confronts our farmers in the three prairie provinces. I gave the total wheat marketing figures for the three prairie provinces. Premier Campbell is not saying that there is a crisis in the prairie provinces. I think that if something is not done soon to find some way to compensate our farmers who are, apparently, only going to be able to sell six bushels this year for a price which is less than half the cost of production, all the prairie provinces are going to be in exactly the same position as the maritime provinces.
Mr. Campbell mentioned in his letter that the inclusion of mental and tubercular costs in the federal share of any hospitalization scheme should be considered, and also a new downward extension of any dominion-provincial unemployment assistance agreements. I was interested to find that the Prime Minister, speaking before the election, made it quite clear that if there was a change of government there would also be a change of policy regarding the inclusion of mental and tubercular patients. Hon. members will
recall that when the Conservatives were on this side of the house they joined with us in criticizing the former administration, pointing out that more than half the people who are sick in bed at the present time are not covered by the so-called national hospital program. We thought it most unfortunate that people who are in tuberculosis hospitals and mental hospitals should be placed in a category different from those who are in general hospitals, and the Conservatives, when they were on this side of the house criticized this policy again and again. Speaking in Winnipeg on May 14 as reported in the Winnipeg Tribune, the Prime Minister said that the Conservatives would repair:
... a "serious omission" in the public health plan which does not include tubercular and mental institutions.
And speaking at Saskatoon on May 27 a few days later, as reported in the Toronto Globe and Mail, he said:
The Conservative party still believes that hospital insurance will cover patients in mental and tuberculosis institutions.
Consequently it is not surprising that Premier Campbell finds it very hard to explain why at this stage the government of the day is suggesting that if the cost of caring for tubercular and mental patients is included they should chisel on other payments to the provinces.
Mr. Campbell points out that Manitoba has bitter memories, not yet 20 years old, of her own near insolvency and starved services. He says:
We have seen other western and some eastern provinces in a somewhat similar plight. For these reasons we urge that any special formulas that might be adopted to provide extra assistance to areas where additional aid is needed (applicable now perhaps only to conditions in the Atlantic provinces) should be applicable wherever in Canada a similar need exists-now or in the future. Let us not have narrow, patchwork, regional settlements. Let us have national plans embracing all parts of Canada.
It is very difficult for people working at municipal and provincial levels to meet the legitimate needs of the people of Canada in the fields of health, education and road construction from the very limited tax resources available to them. The federal government on the other hand is able to collect her taxes easily and freely. The cabinet is presently considering a proposition to spend $1 billion on the development and putting into service of the CF-105. If a decision is reached to spend $1 billion on this type of project there will hardly be insuperable obstacles to surmount with regard to the financial arrangements. We have established before in Canada that a country which kept one million of our able-bodied citizens unemployed week after
3880	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Dominion-Provincial Relations
week and month after month was able, when war broke out, to put one million men in uniform and another million into war industries. We were able to build ships and fill those ships with lumber, food, ammunitions and send them across the Atlantic, and as quickly as we could send them Hitler's submarines were sending them to the bottom of the sea. But in the meantime we were establishing the most prosperous period in Canada's history.
Twenty years after a commission was established to see how best the provinces and municipalities might be assisted through these tax agreements we come to a parliament in January 1958 and are saying that this must be rushed through in the course of a few days before there is an election, or else those who hold up this legislation will be held responsible. You can fool some of the people all of the time, and all of the people some of the time, but you cannot fool all of the people all the time. There is no good reason why we should be confronted today with the need to make a decision on this matter, having already given unanimous consent to deal with the question without the usual 24-hour delay, in order that changes might be made in figures which were placed before us.
I should like to remind the committee of some of the firm commitments which were made with regard to this question by some of the members of the cabinet, particularly the Prime Minister prior to the June election.
The Toronto Star, reporting a speech made by the Prime Minister at Toronto on April 25, has this to say:
Mr. Diefenbaker acknowledged federal-provincial relations were in a "mess" because provinces and municipalities were being handcuffed by inadequate sources of revenue. This was preventing several provinces from discharging their constitutional responsibilities and promoting development of their natural resources. He did not name the provinces he had in mind but it is certain he does not consider Ontario one of them.
A Conservative government, he pledged, would call for an immediate dominion-provincial conference to settle such problems "not in a spirit of arrogant domination displayed by the Liberal government . . . but in a spirit of unity".
The Prime Minister also appeared in an election telecast with the Secretary of State and the hon. member for York-Humber, and again this matter was discussed. He is reported as saying:
And that's one of the serious situations today- the federal government gobbling up the tax dollar. As a matter of fact, in 1949, the municipalities received 29 per cent. Today, they're receiving 11 per cent.
That was a good point to make. These figures vary from time to time but as some

one mentioned this afternoon the municipalities get 11 cents of the tax dollar, the provinces get 14 cents and the federal government gets 75 cents. Sometimes the federal government receives a little more and sometimes a little less but the division about which the Prime Minister complained in that telecast on May 22, 1957 remains unchanged. He has had plenty of opportunity to call together a conference of federal, provincial, and municipal authorities to try and work out some formula under which the municipalities would receive something more than 11 cents and the provinces something more than 14 cents when, as I said, the federal government is able to collect money so easily. Speaking in Minto, New Brunswick, on June 1, 1957, the Prime Minister is reported as having said:
Mr. Diefenbaker promised too that if he is elected Prime Minister of Canada next Monday, his government will call a conference of federal, provincial and municipal officials to see what can be done to ease "the frightful load" being carried by noncentral governments.
Speaking in Cambridge, Nova Scotia on June 3, 1957 the Prime Minister is reported as having said:
I will never participate in anything nor in any way that will bring about disequality in all parts of this country. I believe in a policy in keeping with the responsibilities of national service that will give to every part of this country in a great development plan a reasonable equality of opportunity, and when that conference meets no province will dictate because agreement can only be arrived at by the consensus of all. No province will dominate. There will be no coercion. One principle of that conference will be-domination never, cooperation ever in all parts of Canada to the benefit of all parts of Canada.
I found it interesting to examine the record of Hansard of two years ago when this matter was before the house. The then leader of the opposition, Mr. Drew, as recorded at page 5999 of Hansard of July 16, 1956, said:
A government that fails to seek a solution of this problem and puts this matter into rigid statutory form before there has been approval is a government that is unfit to govern.
I submit that the Minister of Finance who was a member of this house when Mr. Drew spoke those words should have another thought about forcing a proposition of this sort on the ten provinces without giving them a chance to come to Ottawa to discuss with the federal government whether or not the proposition is reasonable, or whether or not something better could be found. The Minister of Finance himself is reported on July 23, 1956, at page 6287 of Hansard as having said:
We are asked to do so with full knowledge that no provincial government has yet given its approval to those proposals and indeed with full knowledge that there has been widespread disapproval of the government's proposals on the ground of their inadequacy.

In spite of this the Minister of Finance is not able to tell parliament today that the premiers have had an opportunity of approving of the present proposal. I continue reading the words used by the Minister of Finance on July 23, 1956 as found at page 6289:
Now, sir, the first subject I think we should refer to in assessing the adequacy of the formula proposed in this bill is what has been the answer of the premiers of the ten provinces of Canada. They are the spokesmen not merely for the provincial governments; they must constitutionally be the spokesmen for thousands of municipalities in this country as well. They have this problem to wrestle with all the time, the problem of inadequate revenues and expanding responsibilities. Every provincial government in Canada has it and every municipal government I have ever heard of has it as well.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, the then minister of citizenship and immigration, interjected that this was not true and the present Minister of Finance went on to say:
There is not one province that has said this provision is adequate.
He then went on to quote at some length from the opinions expressed by the premiers of the provinces at that time but he will be obliged to admit that the premiers were at least there to hear the government of the day make its statements and I suggest that that was much more courteous treatment than was accorded to the premiers by the present government which sent out telegrams followed by a newspaper dispatch a few days later advising the premiers of Prince Edward Island and British Columbia that a most serious mistake in arithmetic had been made by the Minister of Finance or his officials and that consequently all the figures were going to be revised.
As reported at page 6290 of Hansard of July 23, 1956, the Minister of Finance proceeded to quote the words of Premier Frost of Ontario with regard to the proposal:
-we feel strongly that a formula that provides a special payment to all provinces except Ontario fails to meet the special needs of this province.
He then quoted the words of Premier Bennett of British Columbia, as follows:
In so far as they apply to a province like British Columbia which is not dependent on fiscal subsidies, is experiencing an unprecedented growth and requires a greater allocation from the cultivation of income tax fields to keep pace with a development which apart from its provincial worth will yield vast returns to the nation.
Every province has a variety of problems. All these problems should be discussed at a round table conference that might extend over several days. If the commitments which were made prior to the election last June were made in good faith and if those who made them now feel they should keep their
Dominion-Provincial Relations word I believe it is not too late even now to send telegrams to the premiers of the provinces and suggest that such a conference be held as a result of the confusion created in the past few days due to rushing this resolution along and making a mistake in the amounts. Parliament could continue in session and we would excuse the Minister of Finance and as many members of the cabinet as necessary. We got along quite well the other day when discussing other business with very few cabinet ministers present in the house and in respect of a matter as important as finding a solution for the dominion, provincial and municipal financial problems the government should extend an invitation immediately to all the provinces to come to Ottawa with the least possible delay for a discussion of the question to assure the bringing in of better resolutions in the future.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are a few points I should like to make about this important matter which as the hon. member for Quebec East said we welcome on this side of the house. It should be noted, of course, that we do not have the constitutional responsibility of recommending expenditures to parliament. What the hon. member for Quebec East has said will have to be borne in mind in connection with the statement made by the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount, who referred to the regrettable lack of a complete financial statement by the Minister of Finance that would enable us to make a proper assessment as to whether, in the light of the government's over-all obligations, this really represents the kind of interim measure the government actually should make. It may be that in the light of the government's total responsibilities, as it sees them, this is by no means as generous an interim measure as the government suggests and of course the opposite could be the case. But the point is that in the absence of a full financial statement by the government it is not possible for any hon. member in this house or for anyone in the country to make a proper assessment as to whether or not a particular proposed expenditure is one that properly fits into the overall financial obligations that confront the nation at this time.
The Prime Minister is reported as having said in Winnipeg, among other things, when speaking on this interim measure which had been announced by the Minister of Finance:
I am very proud of this plan because it is just one more step along the way toward fulfilling the promises we made.
The fact is, Mr. Chairman, that this is not in any way a fulfilment of the promises which the Prime Minister made during the
3882	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations course of the election regarding the matter of federal fiscal arrangements with the provinces.
The member who has just spoken quoted from several of the speeches made by the Prime Minister, and I should like to quote from one or two others to indicate what the Prime Minister told the people of Canada he was going to do, not in the month of January, not seven months after the government had taken office, but right away, about this matter of dominion-provincial fiscal relations. He predicated his promises on the accepted recognition that good government in Canada depends on satisfactory relations between the two senior levels of government. Indeed, he said that we cannot have good government in Canada unless there is the fullest understanding arising out of the constitutional responsibilities of the two senior levels of government, unless there is a clear opportunity given to each to discharge its functions under sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act.
Then, he said in his opening campaign speech in Massey Hall:
We intend to form a government to immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference to bring about a settlement of these problems.
Two days later he is reported by the Winnipeg Free Press as saying that a Conservative government, if elected, would immediately call a federal-provincial conference, not to explore but to use his exact words, "To settle existing fiscal problems between the dominion and the provincial governments." Then he said in Montreal on April 25:
A Conservative organized dominion-provincial conference would settle this problem ''in a spirit of unity, amity and with mutual tolerance and respect".
What are the facts? The facts are that this conference was first called in November, and it is not going to be reconvened at any date that has been indicated to the provinces or to the house. We do not know whether there is going to be a conference after a federal election, assuming a federal election comes soon, or assuming it comes in June or in September. We have no idea whether that conference is going to be before or after a federal election or whether it is going to be called at all. We have not been told by the Minister of Finance whether or not there will be a conference to bring finality to this matter. I am sure that there are many provincial premiers, certainly the premier of Ontario, who, notwithstanding the satisfaction expressed by him in tonight's paper, will not be satisfied with some $22 million which, under this arrangement and according to this version, is to be accorded to the province of Ontario.


Then, the Prime Minister went on in his statement in Winnipeg and said:
The temporary measure resulted-
And I ask hon. members to note these words:
The temporary measure resulted from the fact his minority government lacked freedom of action and could not carry out the long-term planning necessary to the country.
There is not an hon. member in the house who can subscribe to the validity of the statement made by the Prime Minister in Winnipeg on Saturday. There has been no interference by any opposition group in this house with regard to the discharge by the government of the obligation which it solemnly committed itself when it sought a mandate from the people during the course of the last federal election. There is nothing to prevent this government calling the provinces together tomorrow or next week, as they were called together on two other occasions within the last 12 years while parliament was in session. The government of another day carried on one conference that lasted almost five days while parliament was sitting, and to suggest to the house, as the Minister of Finance did today, that the reason that this conference is not being reconvened is that parliament is now meeting is to suggest something which no hon. member will agree to because my hon. friend knows that this is not the case.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: It certainly is the case.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
My hon. friend and his colleagues have some other reason for not reconvening this conference and it might be worth while examining this reason as we go along. It is true that for this year, at any rate, as the hon. member for Quebec East said, there is the recognition of the principle of equalization; but what happens after this year? Assume there is to be an early election, and while my hon. friends opposite will likely not then have the opportunity of dealing with this matter, it will be interesting to speculate whether or not they would adhere to the principle of equalization if later they did. Why do I say that?
I say that because at the conference itself Premier Campbell, representing one of the provinces that stood to benefit from the principle of equalization, urged the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance in their original statements to recognize this principle. There was no comment whatsoever, certainly in the public session, by either the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance, as to whether or not they recognized this principle of equalization. It is all very well to do so for a year, but that was not the basis on which Mr. Harris presented this

particular formula as a way of bringing about a greater measure of equity as between one province and another.
The Minister of Finance said that among the achievements of the conference in November was the decision reversing the policy that six provinces must have schemes in force before payments by the federal treasury could be provided for under the hospital insurance act. What my hon. friend should have said was that because of the failure of this government to make any progress whatsoever in the matter of hospital insurance this particular amendment became necessary in order not to embarrass the province of Ontario which hopes to begin its scheme on January 1, 1959.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: A very entertaining speech.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Then, the Minister of Finance said that one of the reasons for this plan is that the government was in this way going to do something about unemployment; it is argued this is a way by which something will be done about unemployment. I recall suggesting to the Prime Minister a week ago tomorrow night the words that he had levelled against the former administration when he called upon that government to convene a dominion-provincial conference to deal with unemployment. I used the Prime Minister's own words and I watched him as I used them. I have the suspicion that one of the reasons for this interim measure was that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, hoped, when confronted with their failure to deal with unemployment, to be able to say, "Oh, but we have done something about this problem; why, we have made an interim arrangement with the provinces; we are going to give Ontario alone $22 million." It is true that on Saturday night Ontario was going to receive only $21 million, and it is true that today Ontario is going to be given another $1 million, while the reported amount for Prince Edward Island on Monday is less than what was reported on Saturday.
Does my hon. friend seriously suggest to the house or to the country that in a province like Ontario, where there are over 150,000 men out of work, the $22 million given to this province is going to take care of the problem of unemployment? I do not deny, as the hon. member for Quebec East said, that the provinces have great additional responsibilities in the matter of road building, in the matter of education and so on. Undoubtedly they are hard pressed for the necessary funds to carry on, but my hon. friend clearly demonstrates that he does not understand the severity of the current unemployment problem when he offers this particular interim measure as a corrective
Dominion-Provincial Relations of unemployment. This money given to Ontario will undoubtedly help that province in the discharge of its many functions under the constitution, but it certainly is going to be only a bagatelle in assisting the municipalities or enabling the province to discharge its responsibilities, along with the federal government, towards the unemployed of this country.
When the Premier of Ontario and the Prime Minister of this country, then leader of the opposition, sat side by side at the opening meeting of the campaign in Massey Hall last April, Premier Frost turned to the Prime Minister and said: There sitting in that chair is the man who is going to give Ontario the moneys that it requires and which it has not received from the present administration to enable it to carry out its responsibilities; there is the man. The amount that Mr. Frost wanted was $100 million. Now, Mr. Frost expresses full satisfaction with this interim measure.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: There is a vast difference between $22 million and $100 million; as a matter of fact, I believe it was $118 million. It will be recalled that when it was suggested the Prime Minister was making a deal with Ontario at the expense of the poorer provinces, the Prime Minister rushed out to western Canada to indicate that his statements and that of Mr. Frost had been misunderstood. If Premier Frost had insisted on $118 million, and if he is only now getting $22 million, one has a right to conclude that prior to the announcement of this matter in parliament, the premier of Ontario was told, here is what we propose as an interim arrangement and we hope you will be satisfied for the time being with this particular measure. Was that suggestion made to the premier of Ontario before it was made to his house? Were other provincial premiers advised of the decision which the government announced on Saturday last?

There can be no doubt that when the premiers met here in the month of November they fully

Dominion-Provincial Relations expected they were going to be called back at the beginning of the new year.
We have a statement in Premier Campbell's letter, as recorded at page 3229 of Hansard for January 11, 1958:
If we are able to have this information in advance, Manitoba will be better prepared to discuss the final special Atlantic arrangements which we understand you are planning to put forward for general consideration and acceptance at the next meeting of the adjourned dominion-provincial conference in January of 1958.
The Prime Minister answered that on December 21, and there was no denial by the Prime Minister that there was going to be another conference held at that time. What has happened? Why should the Minister of Finance not be excepted to explain to the provinces and to this house why the dominion-provincial conference is not going to be reconvened at an early date? Why should the Prime Minister and the government not be held accountable for the promises that they made during the election campaign that they would call a conference at once to settle these problems? Why should the Minister of Finance and the government not be asked to explain why they have now gone back on the assurance that the Minister of National Health and Welfare gave in this house and that the Minister of Finance, I think, gave in this house with regard to the inclusion of tuberculosis and mental illness under the hospital insurance act.
Premier Campbell says, as recorded at page 3228 of Hansard for January 11, 1958:
When you promised or implied new financial relief to municipalities and provinces, or when you and your colleagues said that mental and tuberculosis costs should be shared by the federal government in a national health plan, no attempt seems to have been made by you or them to indicate that relief and assistance given on one program would reduce the relief and assistance so badly needed on the other. At no time did you or your colleagues say, for example, that if the provinces wanted mental and tuberculosis costs included in the national health plan, the federal share of such costs would have to come out of the provincial share of any future improvement in tax-sharing arrangements.
Let there be no mistake about this. My hon. friend argued for the inclusion of tuberculosis and mental illness. The Minister of Finance who now sits in discomfort and smiles-

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
The resolution before us at this moment has to do in part with the introduction of a measure to provide for financial assistance to the Atlantic provinces by authorizing certain payments out of the consolidated revenue fund for each of the
Dominion-Provincial Relations four fiscal years commencing on the 1st day of April, 1958. At the outset, Mr. Chairman,
I want to assure the members of this house that I will support this bill and that my remarks at this time will be brief.
The preliminary report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, made public over a year ago, clearly established the fact that the average income in the Atlantic provinces was below the averages for the rest of Canada. People with low incomes are generally found in most rural areas throughout Canada, but such conditions are more widespread in the Atlantic region than in any other section of the country.
We recognize that every dollar of federal revenue comes from Canadian taxpayers and therefore every dollar paid in stabilization or equalization payments is contributed by the same taxpayers. It is therefore in everyone's interest to reduce the differential, if it is at all possible to do so, which now exists between residents of the Atlantic provinces and those in other areas. Since the presentation of the Gordon report the government of Canada-whether we consider the previous administration or the present one-has taken some positive and comprehensive approach to the problems of the Atlantic region. We have, however, serious problems of transportation and communication which have not as yet entirely been taken care of. No one can deny the desirability of granting to the Atlantic provinces some measure of capital assistance which could be used toward the construction of public projects, including transportation facilities. It is generally agreed that the over-all economic position of the Atlantic provinces justifies the special grants which are now being asked for in order to aid the governments of those provinces.
From the implementation of this measure the province of New Brunswick will receive $7| million per year in special grants plus an additional $2 million from the amendment of the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Agreements Act. It may be desirable to relieve the New Brunswick provincial treasury by a special grant of $7J million per year; but unfortunately we also have in New Brunswick a situation which is much more serious than the financial standing of our provincial government.
Here I want to refer briefly to the critical situation which exists in practically all of our municipalities. I am fully aware of the constitutional problems which one may encounter in this particular field. This does not mean, however, that the time has not come for action to be taken without delay to relieve our overtaxed and overburdened municipalities.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
I would dare to say that no other municipality in the whole of Canada has to face today conditions such as those we have in my own municipality of Gloucester. In no other section of the country have the ratepayers to meet municipal and educational taxes which would be nearly as high, percentagewise, as are those which we are being asked to pay in Gloucester county. I believe to a certain extent in the principle of provincial autonomy. I believe in the rights of the provinces and of the individuals with respect to providing and controlling our educational system; but I also believe that there is somewhere a limit to what an individual can pay, notwithstanding his income or sources of revenue.
When, for example, an individual has to pay a municipal and educational tax of $380 per year on a plain, modest $10,000 or $12,000 home, with no sewage or water service or when an ordinary country merchant operating a general store has to pay close to $4,000 a year in municipal taxes, there is something abnormal somewhere, and this situation cannot carry on forever. I know of a country doctor who built a new home in 1955; in fact, he was my first neighbour. Last year his municipal tax bill was $860, and this again with no service such as water, sewage or fire protection. No wonder that a few weeks ago he decided to close his house and has now moved to Ottawa where he is practising.
What about our fishermen? For how long can they keep on, when an individual fisherman, the owner of a fishing dragger, has to pay municipal taxes varying from $700 to $1,000 per year. Here is an individual whose period of earnings is limited to six months a year. During this short period he must earn enough to pay in the vicinity of $1,200 a year for interest on the loan which he received to build his boat; about $400 to $600 a year for insurance protection on his boat; and on top of all this, $700 to $1,000 for municipal taxes.
If these federal grants to the Atlantic provinces are to be of any assistance to the individuals of these provinces, and particularly to the individual taxpayers of the New Brunswick municipalities, at least 50 per cent of such grants should be earmarked as direct grants to the municipalities. This is the only way for all the residents of the Atlantic provinces to benefit from these measures included in the resolution now before us for consideration.
The municipality of Gloucester, with a population of slightly over 60,000 people, has to provide and maintain schools to take care
[Mr. Roblchaud.l

of its 16,000 pupils. Very few municipalities in Canada, in fact I doubt if any other municipalities, have a percentage of children attending school exceeding 25 per cent of its population. Therefore, I would consider that provincial autonomy, indeed freedom of education, would be preserved even if 50 per cent of the special grants for the Atlantic provinces were to be earmarked as direct grants to municipalities. Unless some measure of assistance is provided at once the municipality of Gloucester, as well as other municipalities in New Brunswick, where ratepayers are overburdened with direct and local taxes well beyond their means to pay, will be facing a situation and conditions which could lead to bankruptcy.
How can we improve our economic position when our few industries are bound to meet such heavy taxation? How can we maintain and operate fish processing plants-our main industry-when the only plant located in my own parish of Caraquet has to pay municipal taxes of over $18,000 per year? These conditions cannot carry on much longer and the only possibility of improvement is for the province of New Brunswick to guarantee without further delay and before it is too late that at least 50 per cent of these additional grants will be passed along to the different municipalities of the province, preferably based on the number of children attending public school.
If our present constitution does not justify the federal government in initiating such a proposal, the least the Minister of Finance could do would be to suggest to the Atlantic premiers-or at least to the premier of New Brunswick-that 50 per cent of these special grants be allotted to the different municipalities of the province. If this were done I can assure the minister I would be much more happy in supporting this measure as I would have the assurance that it would benefit every individual man, woman or child, of the province of New Brunswick. My suggestion is, after all, well in line with the Prime Minister's statement made in Winnipeg on last Saturday when he stated that the government expects the larger share of this extra tax revenue to help solve the financial problems of the municipalities.
I sincerely hope this suggestion will be passed along to the premier of New Brunswick with a strong plea to earmark 50 per cent of this amount for the municipalities. I might add that every minister of finance of every province in Canada would welcome this 50 per cent of the extra grants being earmarked to alleviate municipal financial problems if the distribution was left entirely in the hands of the provinces themselves.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS MEASURE TO PROVIDE FINANCIAL ASSISTANCE TO ATLANTIC PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
I would first of all like to pay a really sincere tribute to the Minister of Finance and to the hon. member for Essex East for the quite remarkable manner in which they are able to blot out the past.
I think it is nothing short of remarkable that the Minister of Finance is able to completely divest his memory of the strident remarks of the former member for Eglinton with regard to the actions of the former government in its approach to the provinces and their mutual problems. The hon. member for Essex East similarly seems to have forgotten all about the existence of the former minister of national health and welfare who, as you will recall, used to evade all questions with regard to our national hospitalization plan using, in fact, the very language and the very speeches we hear today from the present Minister of National Health and Welfare.
As I have said previously, I think it is rather a good thing that we cannot copyright our speeches in the House of Commons or there would be a great many interchanges of bills at this particular time for royalties for the use of other people's speeches, and I can only think that if this situation continues and if we have another election which causes another interchange across the floor of this house then some of the leading members in this chamber are going to be suffering from bad cases of schizophrenia before they get through. I am afraid that whether they are sitting on the opposition side or on the government side of the chamber they would have to have their speeches very firmly typed out and clearly marked "opposition speech", "government speech".
I am interested in this move on the part of the government because it does seem to me to be another faltering step in line with the proposal made by this group last week for a redirection of investment. You will remember this was a proposal which caused the great Liberal party to retreat with many shivers of apprehension; not perhaps quite so shivery as they were when they heard the Minister of Finance in his most unsporting way pull another rug from underneath their feet, but nevertheless a faltering step in the direction of re-investment of capital in Canada.
However, I think there are a number of objections which might be raised respecting the way in which the government is going about this business. We, of course, are not in a position to know just what our national bank account is like at the present time, but nevertheless I have the suspicion that we might find ourselves in a rather bad way financially unless these faltering steps which
Dominion-Provincial Relations the government is taking in the way of directing investment into the necessary public fields are balanced by some corresponding action on the other side of the ledger, and I have heard no suggestion from the Minister of Finance that he has any intention of redirecting our economy in that way.
Earlier today I attempted to find out if it might be possible that some of these very large new expenditures are going to be balanced by a curtailment in national defence expenditure but I could not get very much information on that score and still do not know whether in the next fiscal year the Minister of National Defence is going to recommend an expenditure of $1f billion or perhaps $2 billion in that regard or whether the government is going to face realities and make funds available for an even greater redistribution of investment than is proposed in this very modest measure which has now come before us.
What we are really doing now is to attempt to redivide the national pie in a way which will be most pleasing to the largest number of people. In the course of the next few weeks or in the next few months I do not think it is unfair to suggest that if it does not go very much further than that, if it would please a large number of people in the next few months, that is all that can be asked of it.
However, I am going to suggest that we must move much more radically, much more drastically in the field of redirecting the savings of the Canadian people into the places where they are required and that even though the present intention of increasing payments to the provinces may enable the provinces to improve the manner in which they have hitherto carried out their constitutional functions, we will have to go much further in order to deal with the other very serious problems lying ahead of us at the present time. I think this is a place where perhaps some serious basic economic thinking should take place and we should try to understand just why it is we have come full circle again to the condition we were in some 25 years ago. I do not think there is much doubt about it; we are working into that position today, if we have not reached it yet.
As we were informed at great length last week, a trend was in motion more than a year ago which had landed us in this present position and there appears to be no sign that the curve is beginning to go up. I believe that the answer to that can be found in some of the figures published by the dominion bureau of statistics. I was interested the other day to read reports from West Germany, which has always been held before us as a great example of the success of hard work
3888	HOUSE OF
Dominion-Provincial Relations and steady application to business, and now we find that in West Germany, unfortunately, they are suffering from the same ailments that afflict our own economy. They have rising unemployment; they are confronted with a failure of world markets and, in short, they are facing the same problems as we are facing today, and for the same reason, namely that in both West Germany and in Canada we are permitting too large a share of the wealth production to go into the hands of a selective group in our society. I am not dealing now with the ethical or moral aspects of this matter, but purely with the mechanical economic results, and those are the factors which our government is now trying to cope with.
In 1956, the dominion bureau of statistics informs us, corporation profits after deductions amounted to $1,830 million; that of that amount some $765 million was paid out in dividends to the owners of those corporations -the shareholders-leaving a balance of undistributed profits of $1,065 million. In the same year the government permitted depreciation allowances of $1,873 million to go into the treasuries of Canadian corporations, which left on hand for the corporations at the end of 1956 a sum just short of $3 billion, or $3,000 million dollars out of a total wealth production of less than $30 billion. Thus more than 10 per cent of our total wealth production was allowed to accumulate in the form of wealth to be reinvested at the discretion of those who control the corporations of this country.
The picture in 1957 is, so far, only complete for half a year but it shows exactly the same trend. Corporation profits for the first half of 1957 after deductions amounted to $832 million; depreciation allowances amounted to $752 millions. If we make a projection for that year based on the first half of the year we will find that the total sum of money left in the hands of the Canadian corporations to be reinvested at their discretion and in their interest would amount to over $2 billion last year.
I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that those figures should be taken in conjunction with the warning that was given us last year by Mr. Coyne of the Bank of Canada as to the cause of inflation-the rash unplanned boom in capital investment which, he warned, must inevitably end in unemployment and depression if it were allowed to continue. That was only made possible because the previous administration and this administration had permitted these vast sums of money to accumulate in the treasuries of Canadian corporations at the expense of badly needed public expenditures for the welfare of the Canadian people.


I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that the government will eventually be obliged to redirect some of those savings of the Canadian people; that they will have to take some of them back into the hands of the Canadian people, that is, into the Canadian treasury, so that instead of merely providing a few million dollars for the provinces to enable them to carry out, quite inadequately, their constitutional requirements, our federal government would be able to redirect large portions of the savings of the Canadian people to consciously decided social purposes.
I need hardly outline them. Everyone in this chamber knows what they are. Almost every day we hear in this chamber demands for expenditures for extremely worthy and necessary projects in Canada. We hear complaints from the provinces and municipalities; we hear demands for an adequate educational system. I suggest to the committee that we cannot meet those demands and still permit the same fiscal policies to prevail as have prevailed over the last 20 years. I do hope this government, having begun to take the first few hesitant steps, may summon up the courage to grasp this nettle and deal with it; that it may decide that in this crisis in our economy and in our society it will abandon some of the shibboleths that have been mouthed by squawkers for so many years and will cease pretending that these figures represent the results of the operations of an economy which can be called a free enterprise economy; that the government will cease to pretend that our society is governed other than by a few gigantic corporations who set the standards of living for the Canadian people, decide the size and nature of the savings of the Canadian people and decide where those savings should be reinvested. I suggest that this government will have to abandon its former analysis of our society if it is going to weather the storms that lie ahead.
We have heard again and again of the need for quite massive help for our educational system. I am not referring now to any suggestion of federal aid for education; I am suggesting a massive redirection of the savings of the Canadian people, much of which must go towards expanding our educational system. If we are going to survive, it has got to go far beyond merely developing as many technicians and practical scientists as Russia is developing. It must embrace a much larger field than that, and it must dig much deeper into the well springs of our society.
I have always been interested to note the quite savage and vicious enmity which is displayed towards soviet communism in contrast with the complacent attitude shown toward the equal, if not worse, savageries and

evils of the nazi system. I have tried to figure out the reason for this vicious antagonism on the one hand and, in earlier times, the almost indifferent attitude taken to the appalling obscenities of the nazi regime. Of course, it will be said that the reason for this enmity is fear of a military attack on the part of the Soviet union. But I cannot square that with my memories of a military threat from Germany, because I recall that my very earliest memories as a boy were of the Kaiser rattling his sabre at us.
I remember the rise of the Nazis, too, and the military threat and yet we did not have that hatred. The reason we did not have that hatred, to my mind, is that they did not pose a threat to the minds of the people of our country whereas the Russians do. If our economy begins to fail because we fail to-

Mr. Chairman, when I read in Votes and Proceedings the resolution proposed by the Minister of Finance this afternoon it was with mixed feelings that I absorbed line after line of the context. Naturally one is pleased to see that the provinces and particularly the maritimes who need it most are to receive more assistance than previously and in that respect the feeling was one of pleasure. There was a further feeling of pleasure which came from the full realization of the fact that it was because of the constant prodding that took place ever since the beginning of the session in the form of the letters from the premiers of the provinces and particularly letters from the premier of Manitoba; prodding in the form of the stand taken by the provincial governments and in particular by Premier Campbell at the dominion-provincial conference, at which time a most excellent brief was presented; and also prodding by several members of this house including your humble servant that the government is finally coming across with something for the provinces.
You may recall, that it was only a few days ago, on January 17 in fact, that I asked a question of the Minister of Finance as reported at page 3397 of Hansard of that date, in the following words:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. In view of the fact that the government of Manitoba is preparing its budget, can the minister state whether or not any changes are contemplated in the fiscal arrangements for the current fiscal year?
The answer of the Minister of Finance, as reported in Hansard, was:
Mr. Speaker, this would involve government policy, and this is not the time to make any announcement.
It is small wonder that my friend the hon. member for Montmagny-L'Islet was spontaneously prompted to comment on that occasion:
You have no policy.
This is an example of what I mean when I speak of prodding from the opposition. I suppose the Prime Minister would call this type of prodding frivolous questioning. He is quite a man with words and we had a brilliant display of his skill with language in this house just last week. Hon. members will recall, for example, that he wanted an election last week and since the Liberals did not want to take the blame for an election,

Mr. Chairman, I was trying to stick to the subject but the hon. member for Halifax rose and asked a question and I attempted to answer. When an hon. gentleman asks me a question I am inclined to become enthusiastic and attempt to answer even if his question is irrelevant. I cannot help departing from my subject once I am sidetracked by irrelevant questions from the other side of the house. I suppose the hon. gentleman wants us to forget about the barking we heard from the Prime Minister the other day but I would just like to make one observation about it. We very much enjoy those fine sonorous phrases we hear from the Prime Minister from time to time. As a matter of fact most of us can recall reciting similar phrases with great effect at college.
If I may return to the subject, Mr. Chairman, I think it would be worth while to place on the record the opinions expressed by the premiers of the provinces regarding this resolution.
I should like to quote the remarks made by Premier Campbell of Manitoba, according to the Free Press of today. Premier Campbell is reported as saying:
Although new offers will mean considerable extra revenues for Manitoba, he was disappointed in that it fell so far short of what Manitoba had proposed. He criticized the grants for not meeting the provinces' proposal for adopting a 15-15-50 formula and for not being equalized to the yield in the highest province.
On the other hand he was glad to see the principle of equalization maintained for at least one year.
However, he said this:
But Manitoba had expected something more permanent than a year-to-year basis, both from the point of view of equalization and "to the

permanency of provincial revenues". This means that Manitoba, along with the other less wealthy provinces, must continue to be extremely vigilant in seeing that the principle of equalization is not abandoned.
Premier Campbell added:
He felt that Manitoba deserved some of the credit that equalization had been maintained for a year at least.
He was also "greatly concerned" over the government's method of dealing with this matter.
Apparently Premier Campbell was not consulted at all. He just heard the news. I do not know whether he heard it over the radio or through a telegram; but, anyway, he was not asked, would you like this, or would you like that? He was told, this is it. One can understand the remarks of Premier Campbell when he said further:
The provinces were promised another conference. We counted on that to make additional representation and to have an opportunity of discussing the federal proposals, whatever they might be, rather than this method which seems to be not just a case of take it or leave it, as they called the former government's actions in this field, but the imposition upon us of a unilateral decree.
It seems that all we can get from this government is a decree-government by decree a la Diefenbaker! I think it is fair to state that in this measure the Conservative government is simply trying to catch the imagination of the voting public by bringing in this resolution at this time; but surely they do not think the Canadian people are so gullible as not to be able to see through so transparent a pre-election gift. I know that some members on the other side do not agree with this statement. Let us look at a statement that appeared in a very good newspaper, the Winnipeg Tribune, which, in spite of the fact that it is very much a Tory paper, is still an excellent newspaper. Here is a headline which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of Saturday, January 25:
Tories Share the Wealth, Manitoba Gets $3 Million Grant.
One should not forget that Manitoba got over $21 million from the Liberals. I should like to read the first paragraph, Mr. Chairman:
The Conservative government today dropped an $87 million pre-election bombshell into the dominion-provincial issue.
That is what it is. I said earlier that when I read the resolution proposed by the Minister of Finance I read it with a mixed feeling, a feeling of pleasure because of reasons outlined earlier, and also a feeling of disappointment. To be exact, this came out after I asked the Minister of Finance a perfectly legitimate question in this house, at which time the premier of Manitoba had to make an important decision regarding his budget. At that time the minister did not
Dominion-Provincial Relations see fit to give me an answer, although at that time he must have known what the government proposal was.
I had a feeling of disappointment also over the fact that this sudden-it must have been either sudden or the minister knew one week ago-decision of the government can stem from only one desire, the desire to throw some more glitterings, Tory glitter -ings, over the ballot boxes. Just look at the answer of the minister when I asked him about this policy. He said, "this is not the time to make an announcement". No, not 10 days ago, but now that an election is just around the corner this is the time. To think that a Tory responsible government, or one that at least should try to look responsible, should resort to such pre-election bombshells, is a factor that will not escape the attention of the Canadian voters.
A new bait is added to the baits that have been tossed at the Canadian voters throughout the last few months, but it may very well turn out that this will be a turning point in the next election campaign, one which will help turn the side away from the Tories and their bombshells and glitterings to once more a true, sound and responsible Liberal government.
Progress reported.

Halifax
January 6, 1958.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
At the recent dominion-provincial conference special grants to the Atlantic provinces were agreed upon in principle. It was, I believe, understood that the four Atlantic provinces would attempt to reach agreement upon a formula.
Since the conference, officials from the federal Department of Finance visited Halifax, and met with officials from the four Atlantic provinces in order to discuss a formula upon which the special grants to the Atlantic provinces might be based.
It is suggested that the total grants to the Atlantic area be based upon an income deficiency per individual of working age (15-69) from 85 per cent of the national average, multiplied by the revenue ratio of 8.81 per cent, multiplied by the working age group population in the area. This would bring the special grants to the four Atlantic provinces somewhere in the vicinity of $25,000,000, the amount depending upon whether one used a three year or a five year average. The amount, of course, would also be subject to variation as factors might vary through the years. The premiers of the four Atlantic provinces have agreed upon the use of this formula to determine the total grants to the area.
The premiers of the four Atlantic provinces have also agreed that the total grant to the area should be divided among the four Atlantic provinces in the following manner:
Newfoundland	
30	per	centNew Brunswick	
30	per	centNova Scotia	
30	per	centPrince Edward Island ....	10	per	cent
I have been authorized by the premiers of New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince

Edward Island to convey to you their agreement upon this formula for the determination of the size of the special grants to the Atlantic area, and this formula for sharing the grant among the Atlantic provinces. We all hope that the formula agreed upon here will seem appropriate to you and your government. These special grants will be of the greatest assistance to the Atlantic provinces.
Dominion-Provincial Relations On behalf of the four Atlantic premiers, I wish to convey to you our appreciation of your leadership in making these special grants available to the Atlantic provinces. Your sincerely,
R. L. Stanfield
The Right Honourable John G. Diefenbaker, P.C., Q.C., LL.D., D.C.L.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Canada.
